subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Explain the principle, construction, and working of a simple direct current (DC) electric motor. State the function of the split-ring commutator.
answer_key: Principle: A current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a torque and rotates. This is based on Fleming's Left-Hand Rule. Construction: It consists of a strong permanent magnet, an armature coil wound on a soft iron core, a split-ring commutator (two halves of a split ring), and two carbon brushes connected to a DC source. Working: When current flows through the coil, opposite magnetic forces act on the opposite arms of the coil, causing it to rotate. Function of commutator: The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of current in the armature coil every half-rotation, ensuring the coil continues to rotate in the same direction.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: State Faraday's laws of electromagnetic induction. Describe an experiment with a coil and a bar magnet to demonstrate electromagnetic induction and explain how Lenz's law determines the direction of the induced current.
answer_key: Faraday's Laws: (1) Whenever there is a change in the magnetic flux linked with a circuit, an induced emf is set up in it. (2) The magnitude of the induced emf is directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit. Experiment: Connect a coil to a sensitive galvanometer. When a bar magnet is pushed towards the coil, the galvanometer deflects, indicating induced current. When the magnet is pulled away, the deflection reverses. When held stationary, zero deflection is observed. Lenz's Law: The direction of induced current is such that it opposes the very cause or change producing it, in accordance with the law of conservation of energy.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Explain the working principle and construction of an AC generator (dynamo). How does it differ fundamentally from a DC motor in terms of energy conversion and output?
answer_key: Principle: Electromagnetic induction (Fleming's Right-Hand Rule). When an armature coil is rotated in a uniform magnetic field, the magnetic flux linked with it changes continuously, inducing an alternating emf and current. Construction: Field magnet, armature coil, slip rings (two independent rings connected to the ends of the coil), and carbon brushes. Difference: An AC generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy and uses slip rings to output alternating current, whereas a DC motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy and uses a split-ring commutator to maintain unidirectional rotation.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: With the help of a labeled diagram description, explain the working principle, types, and transformation ratio of a transformer. Why can a transformer not be used with a direct current (DC) source?
answer_key: Principle: Based on mutual induction between two coils wound on a soft iron core. Types: Step-up transformer (increases voltage, decreases current, N_s > N_p) and Step-down transformer (decreases voltage, increases current, N_s < N_p). Transformation ratio: V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p = I_p / I_s. Why not DC: A transformer requires a continuously changing magnetic flux to induce an alternating emf in the secondary coil. DC provides a steady, constant current and magnetic field, producing zero flux change after initial switching, hence no secondary emf.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Explain the factors on which the magnitude of the magnetic force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a uniform magnetic field depends. State the rule used to determine the direction of this force.
answer_key: Factors: (1) Magnitude of electric current (I) flowing through the conductor. (2) Strength of the magnetic field (B). (3) Length of the conductor (L) inside the magnetic field. (4) Angle between the direction of current and the magnetic field (maximum when perpendicular, F = BIL). Rule: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule is used. Stretch the thumb, forefinger, and middle finger of your left hand mutually perpendicular to each other. If the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the middle finger in the direction of current, the thumb points in the direction of the force (motion) on the conductor.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Describe the layout of a domestic electric circuit. Explain the functions of the three wires in a household power supply (Live, Neutral, and Earth) and the safety role of an electric fuse.
answer_key: Layout: Power enters through a main fuse and kWh meter into a distribution box with main switches and individual circuit breakers/fuses. Wires: Live wire (brown/red, carries high potential current), Neutral wire (blue/black, completes the circuit returning current), Earth wire (green/yellow, connected to a metal plate deep in the ground to protect against electric shocks by channeling leakage current). Electric fuse: A safety device made of an alloy with low melting point and high resistance. If current exceeds safe limits due to overloading or short-circuiting, the fuse wire heats up, melts, and breaks the circuit, preventing appliance damage or fire.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Compare an electromagnet with a permanent magnet on the basis of any four distinct properties. State two methods to increase the strength of an electromagnet.
answer_key: Comparison: (1) Strength: Electromagnet can produce very strong magnetic fields; permanent magnets have relatively weaker fields. (2) Adjustability: Strength of an electromagnet can be easily varied by changing current or turns; permanent magnet strength is fixed. (3) Polarity: Polarity of an electromagnet can be reversed by reversing current direction; permanent magnet polarity is fixed. (4) Material: Electromagnets use soft iron core; permanent magnets use steel, alnico, oralnico. Methods to increase strength: (a) Increase the magnitude of electric current flowing through the coil. (b) Increase the number of turns of wire in the solenoid or insert a soft iron core inside it.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: State Oersted's experiment and explain what it concludes about the relationship between electricity and magnetism. Describe the pattern of magnetic field lines around a current-carrying straight conductor.
answer_key: Oersted's Experiment: A magnetic compass needle is placed directly below and parallel to a wire connected to a battery and switch. When current is switched on, the compass needle deflects. When current is reversed, the deflection reverses. Conclusion: An electric current flowing through a conductor produces a magnetic field around it, establishing that electricity and magnetism are related. Field lines around a straight conductor: The magnetic field lines form concentric circles centered on the wire, lying in planes perpendicular to the wire. Their direction is given by Maxwell's Right-Hand Thumb Rule.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Explain the working principle and energy losses in a practical transformer. How are these energy losses minimized in transformer design?
answer_key: Principle: Mutual induction where alternating current in the primary coil creates a changing magnetic flux linked with the secondary coil, inducing an EMF. Energy losses: (1) Copper loss (heat loss due to electrical resistance of windings). (2) Eddy current loss (heat loss due to circulating currents induced in the iron core). (3) Hysteresis loss (energy wasted due to repeated magnetization and demagnetization of the core). (4) Magnetic flux leakage (all flux from primary doesn't link with secondary). Minimization: (a) Use thick copper wires to reduce resistance. (b) Use a laminated soft iron core to minimize eddy currents. (c) Use soft iron for low hysteresis loss. (d) Wind secondary closely over primary to minimize flux leakage.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: What is a solenoid? Describe the magnetic field pattern produced by a current-carrying solenoid and state the factors that determine the strength of its magnetic field.
answer_key: Definition: A long, tightly wound helical coil of insulated copper wire whose length is much greater than its diameter. Magnetic field pattern: The field inside the solenoid is uniform and parallel to its axis (resembling a bar magnet), while outside it is weak and divergent. One end acts as a North pole and the other as a South pole. Factors determining strength: (1) Number of turns per unit length of the solenoid. (2) Magnitude of electric current flowing through the coil. (3) Nature of the core material (inserting a soft iron core dramatically increases the magnetic field strength).
rubric_keywords: number of turns per unit length

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow: An AC generator (dynamo) is a device used to convert mechanical energy into electrical energy based on the principle of electromagnetic induction. (ii) Slip rings are used to maintain continuous sliding contact with the rotating coil without reversing the polarity of the output external circuit every half cycle, thus producing alternating current (AC).
(iii) Magnitude of induced emf depends on: (1) Number of turns in the coil, (2) Strength of the magnetic field, (3) Area of the coil, and (4) Speed of rotation of the coil.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow: A transformer is a static electrical device used to step up or step down alternating voltage based on mutual induction. An ideal step-down transformer has 1000 turns in its primary coil and 50 turns in its secondary coil. It is connected to a 220 V AC mains supply.
(i) Define mutual induction.
(ii) Calculate the output voltage across the secondary coil.
(iii) Assuming the transformer is ideal (100% efficient), if the current in the primary circuit is 0.5 A, determine the current in the secondary circuit.
answer_key:
(i) Mutual induction is the phenomenon of inducing an emf in a secondary coil due to a change in current in a nearby primary coil.
(ii) Using the transformer turns ratio formula: $V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p \Rightarrow V_s = V_p \times (N_s / N_p) = 220 \times (50 / 1000) = 220 \times 0.05 = 11\text{ V}$.
(iii) For an ideal transformer, input power = output power: $V_p I_p = V_s I_s \Rightarrow 220 \times 0.5 = 11 \times I_s \Rightarrow I_s = 110 / 11 = 10\text{ A}$.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow: A cylindrical coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wrapped closely in the shape of a cylinder is called a solenoid. When an electric current is passed through a solenoid, it produces a magnetic field similar to that of a bar magnet. The magnetic field inside a long solenoid is uniform and strong.
(i) State two factors on which the strength of the magnetic field inside a current-carrying solenoid depends.

answer_key:
(i) The strength of the magnetic field inside a solenoid depends on: (1) Magnitude of current flowing through the solenoid, and (2) Number of turns per unit length of the solenoid (or soft iron core inside it).
(ii) The polarity is determined by observing the direction of current at the ends. If current flows clockwise, it acts as a South pole; if counter-clockwise (anticlockwise), it acts as a North pole.
(iii) An electromagnet can produce a very strong magnetic field, and its magnetism can be easily switched on or off (or its strength varied), unlike a permanent magnet.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow: A straight conductor of length 0.5 m carrying a current of 4 A is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of magnetic induction 0.2 T.
(i) State the formula for the magnetic force experienced by a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
(ii) Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic force acting on the conductor.
(iii) State the condition under which the force experienced by the current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is zero.
answer_key:
(i) The formula for magnetic force is $F = B \cdot I \cdot L \cdot \sin\theta$, where $B$ is magnetic field, $I$ is current, $L$ is length, and $\theta$ is the angle between the conductor and the magnetic field.
(ii) Substituting the values: $F = 0.2\text{ T} \times 4\text{ A} \times 0.5\text{ m} \times \sin(90^\circ) = 0.2 \times 4 \times 0.5 \times 1 = 0.4\text{ N}$.
(iii) The force is zero when the conductor is placed parallel or anti-parallel to the magnetic field lines (i.e., $\theta = 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$, so $\sin\theta = 0$).

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow: Lenz's Law is a fundamental law used to determine the direction of induced current in a circuit undergoing electromagnetic induction. It states that the direction of the induced current is such that it opposes the very cause (change in magnetic flux) that produces it.
(i) Which conservation law is validated by Lenz's Law?
(ii) A bar magnet is moved towards a closed circular coil with its North pole facing the coil. What will be the magnetic polarity of the face of the coil towards the magnet?
(iii) Explain briefly why Lenz's law must oppose the change in magnetic flux (conservation aspect).
answer_key:
(i) Lenz's Law is a consequence of the Law of Conservation of Energy.
(ii) According to Lenz's law, to oppose the approach of the North pole, the face of the coil towards the magnet will acquire a North polarity (repelling the incoming magnet).
(iii) If the induced current aided the change, it would create perpetual motion violating the conservation of energy, as work done in moving the magnet would continuously multiply without any input energy.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow: In domestic electrical circuits, electricity is distributed through three wires: Live wire (brown/red), Neutral wire (blue/black), and Earth wire (green/yellow). Safety devices like fuses and switches are connected in the live wire.
(i) What is the main function of the Earth wire in a domestic circuit?
(ii) Why is the fuse always connected to the live wire and not the neutral wire?
(iii) State the color coding of the insulation of the Live wire as per the latest standard BIS code.
answer_key:
(i) The Earth wire protects the user from electric shock by providing a low-resistance path for leakage current to flow safely into the ground if the live wire touches the metallic casing of an appliance.
(ii) If a fuse is connected in the neutral wire and a fault occurs, the live wire remains at high voltage even though the current flow stops, posing a severe electric shock hazard. Connecting it to the live wire cuts off the appliance completely from the high-potential source.
(iii) According to the latest BIS color coding standard, the Live wire insulation is Brown (older standard was Red).

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow: Eddy currents are circulating currents induced in bulk pieces of conductors when they are subjected to a changing magnetic field. They often cause undesirable energy loss in the form of heat in transformer cores and electric motors, but are extremely useful in applications like electromagnetic braking in trains and induction furnaces.
(i) Define eddy currents.
(ii) How are eddy currents minimized in the core of a transformer?
(iii) State one practical application where eddy currents are deliberately utilized to advantage.
answer_key:
(i) Eddy currents are loops of electrical current induced within conductors by a changing magnetic field in the conductor, resembling swirling eddies in water.
(ii) Eddy currents are minimized by using laminated iron cores (thin sheets of silicon steel insulated from each other by varnish), which increase the resistance paths and restrict current flow.
(iii) Electromagnetic braking in high-speed trains (or induction heating / induction furnace / dead-beat galvanometer).

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A straight wire of length 0.5 m carrying a current of 4 A is placed at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of magnetic flux density 0.2 T. Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic force acting on the wire.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A solenoid of length 20 cm has 500 turns of wire wound over it. If a current of 2 A flows through the solenoid, calculate the magnitude of the magnetic field inside the solenoid near its center. (Take permeability of free space mu_0 = 4pi * 10^-7 T m A^-1).
answer_key: Formula: B = mu_0 * n * I, where n = N / l = 500 / 0.2 = 2500 turns/m. B = (4 * pi * 10^-7) * 2500 * 2 = 6.28 * 10^-3 T. Magnetic field inside is 6.28 x 10^-3 T.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A step-down transformer operates on a 230 V mains supply and delivers 2 A at 23 V to a device. Assuming the transformer is 100% efficient, calculate (i) the primary current and (ii) the power output.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A conductor of length 1.2 m carrying a current of 5 A is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T at an angle of 30 degrees to the direction of the magnetic field. Calculate the force acting on the conductor. (sin 30 deg = 0.5)
answer_key: Formula: F = B * I * l * sin(theta). Given B = 0.4 T, I = 5 A, l = 1.2 m, theta = 30 degrees. F = 0.4 * 5 * 1.2 * 0.5 = 1.2 N. The force acting on the conductor is 1.2 N.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A transformer has 500 turns in the primary and 50 turns in the secondary coil. The primary voltage is 200 V and the load in the secondary draws a current of 3 A. If the efficiency of the transformer is 90%, calculate (i) the secondary voltage, and (ii) the power input to the primary coil.
answer_key: (i) V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p => V_s = (50 / 500) * 200 = 20 V. (ii) Power output P_out = V_s * I_s = 20 * 3 = 60 W. Efficiency = (P_out / P_in) * 100 => 90 = (60 / P_in) * 100 => P_in = 66.67 W. The secondary voltage is 20 V and power input is 66.67 W.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A straight wire of length 80 cm is kept perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. If a force of 0.48 N acts on the wire when a current of 3 A passes through it, calculate the magnetic field intensity of the field.
answer_key: Formula: F = B * I * l * sin(90) => B = F / (I * l). Given F = 0.48 N, I = 3 A, l = 0.8 m. B = 0.48 / (3 * 0.8) = 0.48 / 2.4 = 0.2 T. The magnetic field intensity is 0.2 T.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A wire of length 25 cm carrying a current of 6 A experiences a maximum force of 0.3 N when placed in a uniform magnetic field. Find the magnetic flux density of the field.
answer_key: For maximum force, theta = 90 degrees. F_max = B * I * l => B = F_max / (I * l). Given F = 0.3 N, I = 6 A, l = 0.25 m. B = 0.3 / (6 * 0.25) = 0.3 / 1.5 = 0.2 T. The magnetic flux density is 0.2 T.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A step-up transformer has a turns ratio of 1:10. If an alternating voltage of 220 V is applied to the primary coil and the current in the secondary circuit is 0.5 A, calculate (i) the secondary voltage, and (ii) the primary current (assuming 100% efficiency).
answer_key: (i) Turns ratio N_s / N_p = 10. V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p => V_s = 10 * 220 = 2200 V. (ii) For an ideal transformer, V_p * I_p = V_s * I_s => 220 * I_p = 2200 * 0.5 => I_p = 5 A. The secondary voltage is 2200 V and primary current is 5 A.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A tightly wound solenoid of length 50 cm has 1000 turns and carries a current of 1.5 A. (i) Calculate the magnetic field at the center of the solenoid. (ii) If the current is doubled and the number of turns per unit length is halved, what will be the new magnetic field at the center? (Take mu_0 = 4pi * 10^-7 T m A^-1)
answer_key: (i) n = N / l = 1000 / 0.5 = 2000 turns/m. B = mu_0 * n * I = (4 * pi * 10^-7) * 2000 * 1.5 = 3.77 * 10^-3 T. (ii) New current I' = 3 A, new turns per unit length n' = 1000 turns/m. New magnetic field B' = mu_0 * n' * I' = (4 * pi * 10^-7) * 1000 * 3 = 3.77 * 10^-3 T. The magnetic field remains unchanged at 3.77 x 10^-3 T.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: What is the SI unit of specific latent heat?
options: Joule per kilogram Kelvin (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
answer_key: Specific latent heat is defined as the heat energy absorbed or released per unit mass during a change of state at constant temperature (Q = mL => L = Q/m). Therefore, its SI unit is Joule per kilogram (J kg⁻¹).

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: The principle of calorimetry is based on which fundamental conservation law?
answer_key: The principle of calorimetry states that assuming no heat is lost to the surroundings, the total heat energy gained by the cold body is equal to the total heat energy lost by the hot body. This is a direct application of the law of conservation of energy.

Ice has a higher thermal conductivity than water.
Water at 0 °C immediately evaporates and absorbs heat.
answer_key: To melt into water at 0 °C, each kilogram of ice must absorb an additional latent heat of fusion equal to 3.36 × 10⁵ J from the surroundings/drink, making ice much more efficient at cooling than water at the exact same temperature.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: During a change of state (e.g., melting of ice or boiling of water), the temperature of the substance remains constant because:
options: Heat energy is no longer being supplied.
The supplied heat energy is entirely utilized in increasing the kinetic energy of molecules.
The supplied heat energy is entirely utilized in breaking intermolecular forces of attraction (increasing potential energy).
The specific heat capacity of the substance becomes infinite.
answer_key: During a phase change, heat energy supplied (latent heat) is consumed entirely to weaken or break intermolecular bonds, increasing the potential energy of the molecules without raising their average kinetic energy (and thus temperature remains constant).

seed_question: The thermal capacity (heat capacity) of a body depends upon:

Surface area and volume of the body

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Two solid spheres A and B of the same mass made of different metals having specific heat capacities cₐ and cᵇ (where cₐ = 2 cᵇ) are heated to the same temperature and then allowed to cool in identical surroundings. Which of the following statements is correct regarding their initial rate of cooling?
options: Sphere A cools faster than sphere B.
Sphere B cools faster than sphere A.
Both cool at exactly the same rate initially.
Rate of cooling cannot be determined without knowing their densities.
answer_key: The rate of fall of temperature (ΔT/Δt) is inversely proportional to the specific heat capacity (c) for equal mass and identical heat loss conditions (ΔT = Q / (m × c)). Since cₐ > cᵇ, sphere B experiences a faster temperature drop per unit heat lost, cooling faster initially.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: State the principle of calorimetry. Explain the underlying physical principle on which it is based and mention two important precautions taken during experiments based on this principle.
answer_key: The principle of calorimetry states that if no heat is lost to the surroundings, the total heat lost by a hot body is equal to the total heat gained by a cold body. It is based on the Law of Conservation of Energy. Precautions: 1. The calorimeter must be properly lagged and polished to prevent heat loss by radiation or conduction. 2. subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Define specific heat capacity and heat capacity. Derive the relationship between them and state their SI units. Also, explain why water has an unusually high specific heat capacity compared to other common liquids.
answer_key: Heat capacity is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of a given body by 1 K or 1°C (SI unit: J K⁻¹). Specific heat capacity is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of unit mass (1 kg) of a substance by 1 K or 1°C (SI unit: J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Relationship: Heat Capacity (C) = Mass (m) × Specific Heat Capacity (c). Water has a high specific heat capacity due to strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding, requiring large amounts of thermal energy to break these bonds and raise kinetic energy.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Explain why water is universally used as an effective coolant in automobile radiators and in industrial heat exchangers. Support your answer with scientific reasoning.
answer_key: Water has a very high specific heat capacity (~4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Because of this high value, it can absorb a large amount of thermal energy with only a relatively small rise in its own temperature. This makes it an exceptionally efficient medium for carrying away heat from engines and machinery without boiling over quickly, acting as an ideal coolant.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Describe an experiment to determine the specific heat capacity of a solid (e.g., a copper block) using a calorimeter. Outline the step-by-step procedure, observations to be recorded, and the final formula used for calculation.
answer_key: Procedure: 1. Weigh the clean, dry calorimeter along with its stirrer (mass m₁). 2. Fill it two-thirds with water and weigh it again (mass m₂), so mass of water is (m₂ - m₁). Note initial temperature T₁. 3. Heat the copper block of mass m₃ to a known high temperature T₂ (using a water bath). 4. Quickly transfer the hot block into the calorimeter and stir well. Record the final steady temperature T₃. Calculation: Heat lost by copper block = m₃ × c_Cu × (T₂ - T₃). Heat gained by water and calorimeter = [(m₂ - m₁) × c_w + m₁ × c_cal] × (T₃ - T₁). Equate heat lost to heat gained to solve for c_Cu.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Distinguish clearly between latent heat of fusion and latent heat of vaporization. Why does a burn caused by steam at 100°C cause more severe damage to human skin than a burn caused by boiling water at the same temperature?
answer_key: Latent heat of fusion is the amount of heat energy required to change unit mass of a substance from solid to liquid at its melting point without temperature change. Latent heat of vaporization is the heat required to change unit mass from liquid to gas at its boiling point. Steam at 100°C contains an additional latent heat of vaporization (~2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹) compared to water at 100°C. Therefore, upon contacting skin, steam releases this extra latent heat during condensation in addition to the heat released during cooling, causing more severe burns.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)

answer_key: During the day, land heats up much faster than the sea because land has a lower specific heat capacity than water. Warm air above land rises, and cooler air from the sea blows toward the land (sea breeze). At night, land cools down much faster than the sea because water retains its heat longer due to its high specific heat capacity. Consequently, warm air rises over the sea, and cooler air blows from the land to the sea (land breeze).

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A piece of ice of mass 40 g at 0°C is added to 200 g of water at 30°C. Calculate the final temperature of the mixture when all the ice has melted. (Specific latent heat of ice = 336 J g⁻¹, Specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹).
answer_key: Heat required to melt 40 g of ice at 0°C to water at 0°C = m × L = 40 g × 336 J g⁻¹ = 13440 J. Heat required to raise this melted ice water from 0°C to final temperature T = 40 × 4.2 × (T - 0) = 168T. Total heat gained by ice = 13440 + 168T. Heat lost by 200 g of water cooling from 30°C to T = 200 × 4.2 × (30 - T) = 840(30 - T) = 25200 - 840T. Equating heat lost and gained: 13440 + 168T = 25200 - 840T => 1008T = 11760 => T = 11.67°C.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Differentiate clearly between heat and temperature on at least four distinct parameters: definition, unit, dependence on mass, and direction of flow.
answer_key: 1. Definition: Heat is a form of energy that flows due to temperature difference; temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body. 2. SI Unit: Heat is measured in Joules (J); temperature is measured in Kelvin (K) or Celsius (°C). 3. Mass dependence: Heat depends on the mass, material, and temperature of the body (extensive property); temperature is independent of mass (intensive property). 4. Direction of flow: Heat always flows from a body at a higher temperature to a body at a lower temperature, whereas temperature determines the direction of heat flow.

To maintain equilibrium, more ice melts. Melting is an endothermic process that absorbs large amounts of latent heat from the surroundings (the mixture and the ice cream container), causing the temperature of the mixture to drop significantly lower than 0°C (down to about -15°C to -21°C), which freezes the ice cream rapidly.

Furthermore, if water freezes, it releases latent heat of fusion. Both processes prevent the ambient temperature around the plants from dropping abruptly below 0°C, thereby protecting crops from ice crystal formation and frost damage.

(iii) Determine the specific heat capacity of the metallic piece.
answer_key:
(i) Water equivalent of a calorimeter is the mass of water whose heat capacity is equal to the heat capacity of the calorimeter. Formula: $W = m \times c$, where $m$ is mass and $c$ is specific heat capacity.
(ii) Heat gained by calorimeter $Q_1 = m_c c_c \Delta T_c = 50 \times 0.4 \times (25 - 20) = 50 \times 5 = 100\text{ J}$. Heat gained by water $Q_2 = m_w c_w \Delta T_w = 200 \times 4.2 \times (25 - 20) = 4200\text{ J}$. Total heat gained = $100 + 4200 = 4300\text{ J}$.
(iii) Heat lost by metal = Total heat gained $\Rightarrow 100 \times c_m \times (100 - 25) = 4300 \Rightarrow 7500 c_m = 4300 \Rightarrow c_m = \frac{4300}{7500} = 0.573\text{ J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.

seed_question:
Read the following passage and answer the questions below:
A calorimeter contains $50\text{ g}$ of water at $50^\circ\text{C}$. $5\text{ g}$ of ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$ is added to the water. The specific heat capacity of water is $4.2\text{ J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ and the specific latent heat of fusion of ice is $336\text{ J g}^{-1}$. Assume negligible heat capacity of the calorimeter.
(i) Calculate the heat energy required to completely melt $5\text{ g}$ of ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$ into water at $0^\circ\text{C}$.
(ii) Calculate the heat energy available from $50\text{ g}$ of water if it cools down to $0^\circ\text{C}$.
(iii) Determine the final temperature of the mixture.
answer_key:
(i) Heat required to melt $5\text{ g}$ of ice: $Q_{\text{melt}} = m_i \times L_f = 5\text{ g} \times 336\text{ J g}^{-1} = 1680\text{ J}$.
(ii) Heat available if water cools from $50^\circ\text{C}$ to $0^\circ\text{C}$: $Q_{\text{avail}} = m_w \times c_w \times \Delta T = 50 \times 4.2 \times (50 - 0) = 210 \times 50 = 10500\text{ J}$.
(iii) Since $Q_{\text{avail}} (10500\text{ J}) > Q_{\text{melt}} (1680\text{ J})$, the ice melts completely and the temperature of the resulting water rises above $0^\circ\text{C}$. Let final temperature be $T$. Heat lost by warm water = Heat gained by melting ice + Heat gained by melted ice raising temperature to $T$. $50 \times 4.2 \times (50 - T) = 1680 + (5 \times 4.2 \times (T - 0)) \Rightarrow 210(50 - T) = 1680 + 21T \Rightarrow 10500 - 210T = 1680 + 21T \Rightarrow 231T = 8820 \Rightarrow T = \frac{8820}{231} = 38.18^\circ\text{C}$.

m_i × c_i × (T_i - T) = m_w × c_w × (T - T_w)
0.5 × 460 × (800 - T) = 1 × 4200 × (T - 20)
230 × (800 - T) = 4200 × (T - 20)

seed_question: 50 g of ice at 0°C is added to 150 g of water at 80°C in a calorimeter of negligible heat capacity. Calculate the final temperature of the mixture. (Specific latent heat of ice = 336 J g⁻¹, specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: 10 g of steam at 100°C is passed into 100 g of ice at 0°C. Calculate the final temperature and composition of the mixture. (Specific latent heat of steam = 2268 J g⁻¹, specific latent heat of ice = 336 J g⁻¹, specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).
answer_key:
Step 1: Heat released by steam condensing to water at 100°C and cooling to 0°C:
- Condensation: 10 × 2268 = 22680 J.
- Cooling from 100°C to 0°C: 10 × 4.2 × 100 = 4200 J.
Total heat released = 22680 + 4200 = 26880 J.
Step 2: Heat required to melt 100 g of ice completely: 100 × 336 = 33600 J.
Since 26880 J < 33600 J, not all ice melts. Final temperature must be 0°C.
Step 3: Mass of ice melted = 26880 / 336 = 80 g.
Composition: Water = 10 g (from steam) + 80 g (melted ice) = 90 g; Unmelted ice = 100 - 80 = 20 g.
Final Answer: Final temperature = 0°C; Mixture composition = 90 g water and 20 g ice.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A copper calorimeter of mass 60 g contains 50 g of water at 20°C. A piece of metal of mass 40 g at 100°C is dropped into it. subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: What is background radiation? State one natural source of background radiation.

seed_question: Distinguish between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion based on the nature of nuclei involved.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Why can gamma radiations not be deflected by an electric or magnetic field?

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A radioactive nucleus undergoes two successive alpha decays followed by one beta decay. What is the change in the atomic number and mass number of the parent nucleus?

A subsequent beta decay increases atomic number by 1 and leaves mass number unchanged. Thus, net change: Atomic number decreases by 3 (4 - 1 = 3), and Mass number decreases by 8.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: What is meant by radioactivity? State two major differences between natural and artificial radioactivity. Mention one important use of radioisotopes in medicine.
answer_key: Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiations (alpha, beta, gamma rays) from the nucleus of unstable atoms during their decay. Differences: Natural radioactivity is a spontaneous process exhibited by heavy naturally occurring elements (like Uranium, Radium) where external factors have no effect, whereas artificial (or induced) radioactivity is the process by which stable nuclei are made radioactive by bombarding them with high-speed particles (like neutrons or protons). Use in medicine: Cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy for treating cancer by destroying malignant cells.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Explain radioactive decay. State the changes that take place in the mass number and atomic number of a radioactive nucleus when it emits: (i) an alpha particle, and (ii) a beta particle. Write balanced nuclear equations for each emission.
answer_key: Radioactive decay is the random, spontaneous breakdown of an unstable atomic nucleus accompanied by the emission of radiation. (i) Alpha emission: Mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number decreases by 2. Equation: ^238_92U -> ^234_90Th + ^4_2He. (ii) Beta emission: Mass number remains unchanged and atomic number increases by 1. Equation: ^234_90Th -> ^234_91Pa + ^0_-1e.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Compare alpha, beta, and gamma radiations on the basis of: (i) their nature, (ii) ionizing power, and (iii) penetrating power. Give the order of magnitude for each.
answer_key: Comparison: (i) Nature: Alpha particles are helium nuclei (^4_2He^2+), beta particles are high-speed electrons (^0_-1e), and gamma rays are electromagnetic waves of very short wavelength. (ii) Ionizing power: Alpha has maximum ionization power (about 10,000 times that of gamma), beta has moderate (about 100 times gamma), and gamma has the least ionizing power. (iii) Penetrating power: Alpha has the least penetrating power (stopped by a thin sheet of paper), beta has moderate (stopped by a few mm of aluminum sheet), and gamma has maximum penetrating power (requires thick sheets of lead or concrete to stop).

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: What is background radiation? State two different sources of background radiation. Why is it essential to follow safety precautions while handling radioactive sources?
answer_key: Background radiation is the ionizing radiation present in the environment from natural and artificial sources, even when no explicit radioactive source is nearby. Sources: Cosmic rays from outer space and naturally occurring radioactive elements in rocks and soil (like radon, potassium-40 in food/water). Precautions are necessary because prolonged exposure to ionizing radiation can damage living tissues, cause genetic mutations, cell death, and lead to cancers or radiation sickness.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Explain why a heavy nucleus tends to be radioactive. How does the emission of an alpha particle and a successive pair of beta particles affect the position of the daughter element in the Periodic Table relative to the original parent element?
answer_key: A heavy nucleus has a large number of protons and neutrons. As size increases, the repulsive electrostatic force between protons increases faster than the short-range attractive nuclear force, making the nucleus unstable and prone to radioactive decay. Effect on Periodic Table: Emission of one alpha particle decreases atomic number by 2 (shifts position two places to the left). Subsequent emission of two beta particles each increases the atomic number by 1, resulting in a net increase of 2 - (1 + 1) = 0. Thus, the final daughter element has the same atomic number as the parent element and occupies the same position in the Periodic Table (they are isotopes).

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Define nuclear fission and nuclear fusion. Write one balanced equation for each process. State one major difference in the conditions required to initiate both reactions.
answer_key: Nuclear fission is the process in which a heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei of nearly comparable masses with the release of a large amount of energy. Equation: ^235_92U + ^1_0n -> ^141_56Ba + ^92_36Kr + 3^1_0n + Energy. Nuclear fusion is the process in which two lighter nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus with the release of immense energy. Equation: ^2_1H + ^2_1H -> ^3_2He + ^1_0n + Energy. Condition difference: Fission can occur at ordinary temperatures using slow neutrons, whereas nuclear fusion requires extremely high temperatures (around 10^7 to 10^8 K) and high pressure to overcome electrostatic repulsion between positively charged nuclei.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: Describe the main components of a nuclear power plant reactor. Explain the specific roles played by: (i) the moderator, and (ii) the control rods in controlling the chain reaction.
answer_key: A nuclear reactor consists of fuel (Uranium-235), moderator, control rods, coolant, and protective shielding. (i) Moderator: Materials like graphite or heavy water are used to slow down fast-moving fission neutrons so that they can effectively cause further fission of U-235. (ii) Control rods: Rods made of neutron-absorbing materials like cadmium, boron, or hafnium are inserted into the core to absorb excess neutrons and regulate the chain reaction, preventing a runaway reaction or meltdown.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: List four important safety precautions that must be observed while handling radioactive substances in laboratories. Explain why radioactive waste must be stored in thick lead casks.
answer_key: Safety precautions: (1) Operators should wear lead aprons and lead-lined gloves. (2) Radioactive substances should never be touched with bare hands; long handle tongs must be used. (3) Sources should be kept in thick lead containers when not in use. (4) Eating, drinking, or smoking should be strictly prohibited in laboratories handling radioactive materials. Lead casks are used for waste storage because lead is a very dense material with high atomic number, offering excellent shielding that absorbs and stops penetrating gamma rays and other radioactive emissions from escaping into the environment.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A radioactive sample emits alpha, beta, and gamma radiations. How would you distinguish between these three radiations using a magnetic field and a photographic plate? Explain the behavior of each.
answer_key: When a beam of radiations is passed through a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the direction of motion: (i) Alpha particles (positively charged) are deflected in one direction in accordance with Fleming's Left Hand Rule, but the deflection is small due to their heavy mass. (ii) Beta particles (negatively charged) are deflected in the opposite direction to alpha particles, and their deflection is very large because they are much lighter. (iii) Gamma rays (electromagnetic waves, uncharged) pass straight through the magnetic field without any deflection. When these separated rays strike a photographic plate placed ahead, alpha and beta produce spots where they hit, while gamma rays produce a dense spot directly opposite the source.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: What is radioisotope tracing? Give two specific applications of radioactive isotopes, one in agriculture and another in industry.
answer_key: Radioisotope tracing is a technique where a small amount of radioactive isotope (tracer) is introduced into a system (biological, chemical, or mechanical) to track its pathway or behavior by detecting the emitted radiations. Agriculture application: Radioisotopes like Phosphorus-32 are used as tracers to study how fertilizers are absorbed by plants and distributed through their roots and stems. Industry application: Radioisotopes are used to detect leaks in underground pipelines or to measure and control the thickness of metal sheets and paper during manufacturing.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A radioactive nucleus $_Z^A X$ emits one alpha particle followed by two beta particles successively. Find the atomic number and mass number of the resulting daughter nucleus.
answer_key: Step 1: Emission of one alpha particle ($_2^4 \alpha$) decreases the mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2. Resulting nucleus: $_{Z-2}^{A-4}X'$. Step 2: Emission of each beta particle ($_{-1}^0 \beta$) increases the atomic number by 1 while mass number remains unchanged. Two beta particles increase atomic number by 2. Final atomic number = $(Z - 2) + 2 = Z$. Final mass number = $A - 4$. Final daughter nucleus is $_Z^{A-4}X''$.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A nucleus of radium $_88^{226}Ra$ undergoes alpha decay to form a daughter nucleus $Y$. Determine the atomic number and mass number of $Y$.
answer_key: Step 1: An alpha particle is represented as $_2^4 \alpha$. Step 2: In alpha decay, mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number decreases by 2. Step 3: Mass number of $Y$ = $226 - 4 = 222$. Atomic number of $Y$ = $88 - 2 = 86$. Final Answer: Atomic number = 86, Mass number = 222.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: During a radioactive transformation, a parent nucleus $_92^{238}U$ emits 3 alpha particles and 2 beta particles. Calculate the final atomic number and mass number of the resulting stable nucleus.
answer_key: Step 1: Initial nucleus has mass number $A = 238$ and atomic number $Z = 92$. Step 2: Emission of 3 alpha particles decreases mass number by $3 \times 4 = 12$ and atomic number by $3 \times 2 = 6$. Step 3: Emission of 2 beta particles does not change mass number and increases atomic number by $2 \times 1 = 2$. Step 4: Final mass number = $238 - 12 = 226$. Final atomic number = $92 - 6 + 2 = 88$. Final Answer: Mass number = 226, Atomic number = 88.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: An unknown radioactive element $_Z^A X$ transforms into stable lead $_82^{206}Pb$ by the emission of 8 alpha particles and 6 beta particles. Determine the initial atomic number ($Z$) and mass number ($A$) of element $X$.
answer_key: Step 1: Let initial nucleus be $_Z^A X$ and final nucleus be $_{82}^{206}Pb$. Step 2: Total change in mass number due to 8 alpha particles = $8 \times 4 = 32$ (beta particles do not affect mass number). Therefore, $A - 32 = 206 \implies A = 206 + 32 = 238$. Step 3: Total change in atomic number due to 8 alpha particles = $8 \times (-2) = -16$ and due to 6 beta particles = $6 \times (+1) = +6$. Net change in atomic number = $-16 + 6 = -10$. Therefore, $Z - 10 = 82 \implies Z = 82 + 10 = 92$. Final Answer: $A = 238$, $Z = 92$.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A radioactive substance $_90^{232}Th$ emits an alpha particle, followed by a beta particle, and then another alpha particle. Determine the atomic number and mass number of the final nucleus.
answer_key: Step 1: Initial nucleus is $_90^{232}Th$. Step 2: First emission (alpha particle): Mass number = $232 - 4 = 228$, Atomic number = $90 - 2 = 88$. Step 3: Second emission (beta particle): Mass number remains $228$, Atomic number = $88 + 1 = 89$. Step 4: Third emission (alpha particle): Mass number = $228 - 4 = 224$, Atomic number = $89 - 2 = 87$. Final Answer: Mass number = 224, Atomic number = 87.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A nucleus $_84^{218}Po$ emits one alpha particle to become nucleus $Q$, which then emits one beta particle to become nucleus $R$. Find the atomic number and mass number of nucleus $R$.
answer_key: Step 1: Initial nucleus is $_84^{218}Po$. Step 2: Emission of 1 alpha particle gives nucleus $Q$ with mass number $218 - 4 = 214$ and atomic number $84 - 2 = 82$ ($_82^{214}Q$). Step 3: Emission of 1 beta particle from $Q$ gives nucleus $R$ with mass number remaining $214$ and atomic number $82 + 1 = 83$ ($_83^{214}R$). Final Answer: Mass number of $R$ = 214, Atomic number of $R$ = 83.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: In a radioactive series, a nucleus $_92^{235}U$ undergoes radioactive decay to form $_82^{207}Pb$. Calculate the number of alpha particles ($n_\alpha$) and beta particles ($n_\beta$) emitted during this process.
answer_key: Step 1: Equate the change in mass numbers. Initial mass number = 235, final mass number = 207. Change in mass number = $235 - 207 = 28$. Since only alpha particles affect mass number, $4 \times n_\alpha = 28 \implies n_\alpha = 7$. Step 2: Equate the change in atomic numbers. Initial atomic number = 92, final atomic number = 82. Total change due to 7 alpha particles = $7 \times (-2) = -14$. Let $n_\beta$ be the number of beta particles. $92 - 14 + n_\beta = 82 \implies 78 + n_\beta = 82 \implies n_\beta = 4$. Final Answer: $n_\alpha = 7$, $n_\beta = 4$.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A radioactive isotope of bismuth, $_83^{214}Bi$, emits a beta particle. Find the mass number and atomic number of the daughter nucleus formed.
answer_key: Step 1: Beta decay involves the emission of an electron ($_{-1}^0 \beta$), where a neutron converts into a proton. Step 2: Mass number remains unchanged ($214$). Step 3: Atomic number increases by 1 ($83 + 1 = 84$). Final Answer: Mass number = 214, Atomic number = 84.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: If a radioactive nucleus $_90^{234}Th$ emits 2 beta particles successively, what will be the atomic number and mass number of the final daughter nucleus?
answer_key: Step 1: Initial nucleus is $_90^{234}Th$. Step 2: Emission of each beta particle increases the atomic number by 1 and leaves the mass number unchanged. Step 3: Two beta particles increase atomic number by $2 \times 1 = 2$. Final atomic number = $90 + 2 = 92$. Final mass number remains $234$. Final Answer: Mass number = 234, Atomic number = 92.

subject: Physics (Science Paper 1)
seed_question: A parent nucleus $_88^{224}Ra$ emits 2 alpha particles and 1 beta particle. Calculate the atomic number and mass number of the final daughter nucleus.
answer_key: Step 1: Initial nucleus: $A = 224$, $Z = 88$. Step 2: Emission of 2 alpha particles reduces mass number by $2 \times 4 = 8$ and atomic number by $2 \times 2 = 4$. Step 3: Emission of 1 beta particle increases atomic number by 1 and does not change mass number. Step 4: Final mass number = $224 - 8 = 216$. Final atomic number = $88 - 4 + 1 = 85$. Final Answer: Mass number = 216, Atomic number = 85.

Step 2: Determine simplest atomic ratio by dividing by the smallest value (3.226). C = 3.226 / 3.226 = 1; H = 9.67 / 3.226 = 3; O = 3.226 / 3.226 = 1. Empirical formula = CH3O. Step 3: Calculate empirical formula mass = (1 \times 12) + (3 \times 1) + (1 \times 16) = 31 g/mol. Step 4: Find 'n' factor = Molecular mass / Empirical formula mass = 62 / 31 = 2. Step 5: Molecular formula = (Empirical formula) \times n = (CH3O)2 = C2H6O2 (Ethylene glycol).

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: (a) State Gay-Lussac's Law of Combining Volumes. (b) State Avogadro's Law. (c) Using Avogadro's Law, deduce the atomicity of hydrogen gas, proving that a hydrogen molecule is diatomic.
answer_key: (a) Gay-Lussac's Law states that when gases react together, they do so in volumes which bear a simple whole number ratio to one another and to the volume of the products, provided all volumes are measured under the same conditions of temperature and pressure. (b) Avogadro's Law states that equal volumes of all gases under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal number of molecules. (c) Proof: Let 1 volume of hydrogen react with 1 volume of chlorine to form 2 volumes of hydrogen chloride gas. $H_2 + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2HCl$. By Gay-Lussac's Law: 1 vol of $H_2$ + 1 vol of $Cl_2$ $\rightarrow$ 2 vol of $HCl$. Let 1 volume contain $n$ molecules. So, $n$ molecules of $H_2$ + $n$ molecules of $Cl_2$ $\rightarrow$ $2n$ molecules of $HCl$. Dividing by $n$: 1 molecule of $H_2$ + 1 molecule of $Cl_2$ $\rightarrow$ 2 molecules of $HCl$. Since each molecule of $HCl$ contains 1 atom of hydrogen, 2 molecules of $HCl$ contain 2 atoms of hydrogen. Therefore, 1 molecule of hydrogen must contain 2 atoms, proving its atomicity is 2 (diatomic).

Quantitative significance: 1. In terms of moles: 1 mole of methane reacts with 2 moles of oxygen to give 1 mole of carbon dioxide and 2 moles of water. 2. subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: (a) Explain the term 'Mole' and state Avogadro's number. (b) Calculate: (i) The number of moles in 12.8 g of sulphur dioxide ($SO_2$). (ii) The mass of $3.011 \times 10^{23}$ molecules of carbon dioxide ($CO_2$). [Atomic masses: S = 32, O = 16, C = 12, Avogadro's number = $6.022 \times 10^{23}$]
answer_key: (a) A mole is the amount of a substance that contains as many elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions, etc.) as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12 ($^{12}C$). Avogadro's number ($N_A$) is the number of particles present in one mole of any substance, equal to $6.022 \times 10^{23}$. (b) (i) Molar mass of $SO_2 = 32 + (2 \times 16) = 64\text{ g/mol}$. Number of moles = $\text{Given mass} / \text{Molar mass} = 12.8 / 64 = 0.2\text{ moles}$. (ii) Molar mass of $CO_2 = 12 + (32) = 44\text{ g/mol}$. Number of moles = $\text{Given molecules} / N_A = (3.011 \times 10^{23}) / (6.022 \times 10^{23}) = 0.5\text{ moles}$. Mass = $\text{Moles} \times \text{Molar mass} = 0.5 \times 44 = 22\text{ g}$.

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: Explain the rules for writing a chemical formula using the valency method. Illustrate with the examples of magnesium chloride and aluminium oxide.
answer_key: Rules for writing a chemical formula: 1. Write the symbols of the constituent elements/radicals side by side, with the electropositive (metal/positive radical) on the left and the electronegative (non-metal/negative radical) on the right. 2. Write their respective valencies or charges on top of each symbol. 3. If the valencies have a common factor, divide to reduce them to the simplest whole number ratio. 4. Criss-cross the reduced valencies and write them as subscripts to the opposite symbol (ignore the positive/negative signs). If the subscript is 1, it is omitted. If a radical has a subscript other than 1, enclose it in parentheses. Illustrations: Magnesium chloride: Symbols $Mg$ and $Cl$, valencies $+2$ and $-1$. Criss-crossed subscripts: $Mg_1Cl_2$, formula is $MgCl_2$. Aluminium oxide: Symbols $Al$ and $O$, valencies $+3$ and $-2$. Criss-crossed subscripts: $Al_2O_3$.

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: Calculate the relative molecular mass of hydrated copper(II) sulphate, CuSO4.5H2O. (Given atomic masses: Cu = 63.5, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1).

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: Calculate the percentage of water of crystallization in washing soda crystals, Na2CO3.10H2O. (Given atomic masses: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16, H = 1).

Total molar mass of Na2CO3.10H2O = 106 + 180 = 286 g/mol. Percentage of water of crystallization = (Mass of water / Total molar mass) * 100 = (180 / 286) * 100 = 62.94%.

answer_key: A chemical change is a permanent change in which one or more new substances with entirely different physical and chemical properties are formed. Two main characteristics: 1. It is generally irreversible. 2. There is a definite exchange of energy (heat, light, etc.).

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: Explain why 'melting of ice' is considered a physical change while 'burning of magnesium ribbon' is a chemical change.
answer_key: Melting of ice is a physical change because no new substance is formed (only state changes from solid to liquid) and it can be easily reversed by cooling. Burning of magnesium ribbon is a chemical change because magnesium reacts with oxygen to form a new substance, magnesium oxide, with different properties, and the change is permanent and irreversible.

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: Differentiate between an exothermic reaction and an endothermic reaction, giving one example of each.
answer_key: An exothermic reaction is a chemical reaction in which heat is evolved or released (e.g., burning of carbon or reaction of quicklime with water). An endothermic reaction is a chemical reaction in which heat is absorbed (e.g., heating of calcium carbonate or reaction between nitrogen and oxygen at high temperatures).

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: What is a catalyst? Distinguish between a positive catalyst and a negative catalyst with suitable examples.
answer_key: A catalyst is a chemical substance that alters the rate of a chemical reaction without itself undergoing any chemical change at the end of the reaction. A positive catalyst speeds up a reaction (e.g., manganese dioxide in the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide). A negative catalyst slows down or retards a reaction (e.g., phosphoric acid or glycerol added to hydrogen peroxide to slow down its decomposition).

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: Define thermal dissociation. How does it differ from thermal decomposition?
answer_key: Thermal dissociation is a reversible chemical change in which a substance dissociates into two or more simpler substances upon heating and recombines on cooling (e.g., dissociation of ammonium chloride). Thermal decomposition is a permanent, irreversible chemical change where a compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances upon heating and cannot recombine on cooling (e.g., decomposition of calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide).

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: Define a chemical change. State any four characteristic properties that help us identify whether a chemical change has taken place, giving one suitable example for each.
answer_key: A chemical change is a permanent change in which one or more new substances with entirely different chemical composition and properties are formed. Four characteristics: (1) Evolution of gas: Action of dilute hydrochloric acid on zinc granules evolves hydrogen gas (Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2↑). (2) Change in colour: When green copper carbonate is heated, it changes to black copper oxide (CuCO3 -> CuO + CO2). (3) Change in temperature: Dissolution of quicklime in water releases a large amount of heat (CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + Heat). (4) Formation of a precipitate: Mixing solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulfate produces a white precipitate of barium sulfate (BaCl2 + Na2SO4 -> BaSO4↓ + 2NaCl).

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: What are the essential conditions required for a chemical reaction to take place? Explain any four conditions with suitable examples.
answer_key: The essential conditions for a chemical reaction are: (1) Close contact: Dry lead nitrate and dry potassium iodide do not react when mixed, but when their aqueous solutions are mixed, they react to form a yellow precipitate of lead iodide. (2) Solution state: Solid sodium chloride and solid sulfuric acid do not react, but concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium chloride when heated. (3) Action of heat: Many decomposition reactions require heat, e.g., thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. (4) Action of light: Photosynthesis in plants or decomposition of silver chloride in sunlight requires light energy (2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2 in presence of sunlight). (5) Action of electricity: Water acidified with sulfuric acid decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen on passing electric current.

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: Classify chemical reactions into four major types based on the nature of the change. Give a balanced chemical equation and one specific example for each type.
answer_key: The four major types of chemical reactions are: (1) Direct Combination (Synthesis) reaction: Two or more substances combine to form a single new substance. Example: Burning of magnesium ribbon in air. Equation: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. (2) Decomposition reaction: A single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances under specific conditions. Example: Thermal decomposition of copper carbonate. Equation: CuCO3 -> CuO + CO2. (3) Displacement reaction: A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its salt solution. Example: Iron displacing copper from copper sulfate solution. Equation: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. (4) Double Displacement (Metathesis) reaction: Two compounds exchange their radicals to form two new compounds. Example: Reaction between barium chloride and sodium sulfate. Equation: BaCl2 + Na2SO4 -> BaSO4↓ + 2NaCl.

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: Explain what is meant by exothermic and endothermic reactions with the help of one example and thermochemical representation for each.
answer_key: Exothermic reactions are those chemical reactions in which heat is evolved or released into the surroundings. Example: Burning of carbon or formation of slaked lime from quicklime. Representation: C + O2 -> CO2 + Heat (or ΔH = -ve). Endothermic reactions are those chemical reactions in which heat is absorbed from the surroundings. Example: Formation of nitric oxide from nitrogen and oxygen at high temperature. Representation: N2 + O2 - Heat -> 2NO (or N2 + O2 -> 2NO - Heat, or ΔH = +ve).

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: What is a catalyst? Distinguish between positive catalysis and negative catalysis with suitable examples. Also, mention the role of catalytic promoters and catalytic poisons.
answer_key: A catalyst is a chemical substance that alters the speed of a chemical reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change at the end of the reaction. (1) Positive catalysis: Speeds up a reaction. Example: Manganese dioxide (MnO2) increases the rate of decomposition of potassium chlorate. (2) Negative catalysis: Slows down or retards a reaction. Example: Phosphoric acid (H3PO4) or glycerol acts as a negative catalyst for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. (3) Catalytic promoters: Substances that enhance the activity of a catalyst. Example: Molybdenum (Mo) acts as a promoter for iron catalyst in Haber's process. (4) Catalytic poisons: Substances that decrease or destroy the activity of a catalyst. Example: Carbon monoxide or sulfur compounds poison the iron catalyst in Haber's process.

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: Explain photochemical reactions and electrochemical reactions with two distinct examples for each, including necessary balanced chemical equations.
answer_key: Photochemical reactions are chemical reactions that take place in the presence of light energy. Examples: (1) Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 (in presence of sunlight and chlorophyll). (2) Photolysis of silver chloride: 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2 (in sunlight). Electrochemical reactions are chemical reactions that take place due to the passage of electric current or produce electricity. Examples: (1) Electrolysis of acidified water: 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2 (on passing electric current). (2) Electrolysis of aqueous copper sulfate solution using copper electrodes.

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: State the differences between a physical change and a chemical change under any three distinct parameters.
answer_key: Differences between physical and chemical changes: (1) Nature of change: Physical change is temporary and reversible, whereas chemical change is permanent and generally irreversible. (2) Formation of new substances: No new substance is formed in a physical change; the chemical composition remains the same. In a chemical change, one or more entirely new substances with different properties are formed. (3) Energy change: Heat or light is usually not absorbed or evolved significantly in a physical change (except during change of state), whereas a definite amount of heat, light, or electrical energy is invariably absorbed or evolved in a chemical change.

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: Define thermal dissociation. Give two examples of thermal dissociation reactions and explain how thermal dissociation differs from thermal decomposition.
answer_key: Thermal dissociation is a reversible decomposition reaction brought about by heat, in which a substance splits up into simpler substances, which recombine on cooling to form the original substance. Examples: (1) Dissociation of ammonium chloride: NH4Cl ⇌ NH3 + HCl. (2) Dissociation of nitrogen tetroxide: N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2. Difference from thermal decomposition: Thermal decomposition is an irreversible chemical change where a compound breaks down into simpler substances that cannot recombine to form the original substance under normal conditions (e.g., CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2), whereas thermal dissociation is a reversible physical/chemical equilibrium process where products recombine on cooling.

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: What is meant by precipitation reaction? Describe an experiment with balanced chemical equation and observation to illustrate the formation of a precipitate.
answer_key: A precipitation reaction is a type of double displacement reaction in which mixing two clear, aqueous solutions results in the formation of an insoluble solid product called a precipitate. Experiment: Take a clean test tube containing aqueous solution of barium chloride (BaCl2) and add a few drops of dilute sulfuric acid or sodium sulfate solution (Na2SO4) to it. Observation: An immediate dense white precipitate of barium sulfate is formed which is insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid. Balanced equation: BaCl2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) -> BaSO4↓ + 2NaCl(aq).

subject: Chemistry (Science Paper 2)
seed_question: Explain the term displacement reaction with two examples: one involving a metal displacing another metal from its salt solution, and another involving a non-metal displacing another non-metal from its compound. Write balanced equations for both.
answer_key: A displacement reaction is a chemical reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound (salt solution). (1) Metal displacement: When a polished iron nail is dipped in a blue-coloured copper sulfate solution, iron displaces copper because iron is more reactive than copper. The blue solution turns pale green (ferrous sulfate) and a reddish-brown coating of copper is deposited on the iron nail. Equation: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. (2) Non-metal displacement: When chlorine gas is bubbled through a solution of potassium iodide, chlorine (being a more reactive halogen) displaces iodine. Equation: Cl2 + 2KI -> 2KCl + I2.
