Dendrites: Short, branched projections that receive nerve impulses. 3. Axon: A single, long, cylindrical process ending in nerve terminals that transmits impulses away from the cell body.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Explain the classification of plant tissues based on their dividing capacity. Describe the three types of meristematic tissues with their specific locations and functions in plants.
answer_key: Plant tissues are broadly classified into two main types based on their ability to divide: Meristematic tissues and Permanent tissues. Meristematic tissues consist of actively dividing cells and are responsible for plant growth. They are further divided into three types: 1. Apical Meristem: Located at the growing tips of roots and stems (shoots); function is primary growth, increasing the length of the plant body. 2. Lateral Meristem (Cambium): Located beneath the bark and in vascular bundles of dicot roots and stems; function is secondary growth, increasing the girth or thickness of the stem/root. 3. Intercalary Meristem: Located at the base of leaves or internodes (e.g., below nodes in grasses); function is the elongation of internodes and regrowth of grazed parts.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Compare the three types of simple permanent plant tissues—parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma—on the basis of their cell wall thickening, living/dead nature, and primary functions.
answer_key: 1. Parenchyma: Cells are living with thin cell walls made of cellulose. Intercellular spaces are present. Functions include food storage, photosynthesis (chlorenchyma), and buoyancy in aquatic plants (aerenchyma). 2. Collenchyma: Cells are living with unevenly thickened cell walls at the corners due to pectin and cellulose deposition. Intercellular spaces are generally absent. Function is to provide mechanical support, flexibility, and elasticity to growing parts like young stems and petiole of leaves. 3. Sclerenchyma: Cells are dead at maturity with uniformly thick, lignified secondary cell walls. Intercellular spaces are absent. Function is to provide rigidity, strength, and mechanical protection to plant parts (e.g., coconut husk, seed coats).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Describe the structure and components of Xylem and Phloem. How do these two complex permanent tissues differ in their function and transport mechanisms in plants?
answer_key: Xylem and Phloem are complex permanent tissues made of more than one type of cell working together for transport. Xylem components: Tracheids, vessels (dead, lignified tubes for upward water and mineral transport from roots), xylem parenchyma (living, stores food), and xylem fibres (dead, provide mechanical support). Phloem components: Sieve tubes, companion cells (living cells responsible for food translocation), phloem parenchyma (storage), and phloem fibres (mechanical support). Difference: Xylem conducts water and inorganic minerals upward from roots to leaves, whereas phloem conducts organic food (sugars synthesized during photosynthesis) bidirectionally from source to sink.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Classify animal tissues into four primary types. Give a detailed account of Epithelial tissue, mentioning its types, structure, and major functions in the animal body.
answer_key: Animal tissues are broadly classified into four primary types: Epithelial tissue, Connective tissue, Muscular tissue, and Nervous tissue. Epithelial tissue forms the covering or protective barrier of the outer surfaces, organs, and cavities inside the body. Cells are tightly packed with minimal intercellular matrix resting on a basement membrane. Types of epithelium: Squamous (thin, flat, tile-like, found in alveoli and blood vessels), Cuboidal (cube-like, found in kidney tubules and glands), Columnar (tall, pillar-like, found in the lining of stomach and intestine), Ciliated (possesses hair-like cilia, found in respiratory tract), and Glandular (secretes substances). Major functions include protection, absorption, secretion, and sensory reception.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: What are connective tissues? Describe the structure, matrix nature, and specific functions of blood, bone, and cartilage as specialized connective tissues.
answer_key: Connective tissues bind, support, and pack together other tissues and organs of the body. They have cells embedded in an extracellular matrix. 1. Blood: A fluid connective tissue with a liquid matrix called plasma, containing red blood cells (RBCs/erythrocytes), white blood cells (WBCs/leukocytes), and platelets (thrombocytes). Function: transport of oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, hormones, and waste products, and defense against pathogens. 2. Bone: A rigid connective tissue with a hard, calcified matrix rich in calcium and phosphorus salts, and collagen fibres. Cells are osteocytes in lacunae. Function: provides skeletal framework, body shape, protection for vital organs, and support for muscles. 3. Cartilage: A semi-rigid, flexible connective tissue with a solid protein-sugar matrix (chondrin) and chondrocytes. Function: cushions joints, reduces friction, and supports flexible body parts like the nose tip, ear pinna, and trachea rings.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Differentiate between skeletal (striated), smooth (unstriated), and cardiac muscle tissues based on their structure, location, and control mechanism.
answer_key: 1. Skeletal (Striated/Voluntary) Muscle: Cells are long, cylindrical, unbranched, and multinucleated with alternate light and dark bands (striations). Location: Attached to bones (e.g., limbs, body wall). Control: Voluntary (under conscious control). 2. Smooth (Unstriated/Involuntary) Muscle: Cells are spindle-shaped (tapering at ends), uninucleated, and lack striations. Location: Walls of hollow internal visceral organs like the alimentary canal, blood vessels, and urinary bladder. Control: Involuntary (not under conscious control). 3. Cardiac Muscle: Cells are cylindrical, branched, uninucleated, and striated, connected by intercalated discs. Location: Walls of the heart. Control: Involuntary (rhythmic contraction and relaxation throughout life without fatigue).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Draw a well-labeled diagram of a nerve cell (neuron) and explain its structure and functional significance in the transmission of nerve impulses.
answer_key: Nervous tissue is specialized for receiving stimuli and transmitting messages across the body. A neuron consists of three main parts: 1. Cyton (Cell Body): Contains cytoplasm and a central nucleus, with Nissl's granules. 2. Dendrites: Short, branched hair-like projections arising from the cyton that receive electrical impulses from other neurons or receptors. 3. Axon: A long, single fibre that transmits impulses away from the cyton. It may be covered by a myelin sheath (Schwann cells) interrupted at nodes of Ranvier. Functional significance: Neurons transmit information rapidly via electrical and chemical signals (nerve impulses), enabling rapid coordination and response to environmental stimuli.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: State five major differences between plant tissues and animal tissues, taking into account their nutritional requirements, growth patterns, and structural support.
answer_key: Five major differences between plant and animal tissues: 1. Growth Pattern: Plant tissues show localized growth restricted to meristematic regions, continuing throughout life. Animal tissue growth is uniform throughout the body and stops after reaching maturity. 2. Dead vs Living Support: Plant tissues contain a large proportion of dead cells (sclerenchyma, xylem vessels) providing structural rigidity. Animal tissues consist mostly of living cells, with minimal dead extracellular structural components (like hair or nails). 3. Energy Requirement: Plant tissues require less energy as plants are stationary and autotrophic. Animal tissues require more energy due to locomotion and heterotrophic metabolism. 4. Differentiation: Plant tissues are simpler in organization with fewer tissue types. Animal tissues are more complex and specialized with nervous and muscular systems. 5. Support Function: Plants need thick-walled dead tissues for standing upright against gravity, whereas animals rely on skeletal and muscular systems for support and movement.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Explain the concept of tissue differentiation and give an account of how meristematic tissues transform into permanent tissues in plants during development.
answer_key: Differentiation is the process by which newly formed cells derived from division of meristematic tissues take up a permanent shape, size, and specific function, losing their ability to divide. Process of transformation: Cells produced by the apical or lateral meristems initially have dense cytoplasm, thin cellulosic walls, and large nuclei. As they mature and move away from the meristematic zone, they undergo structural and chemical modifications (differentiation). For example, some cells deposit extra cellulose or lignin and lose their protoplasm to become dead sclerenchyma or xylem vessels for support and conduction. Others retain living protoplasm, develop thin walls, and specialize in photosynthesis or food storage (parenchyma). This division of labor increases the efficiency of the plant body.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Describe the location, structure, and functions of adipose tissue and areolar tissue in animals. How do these supportive and packing tissues help maintain homeostasis?
answer_key: 1. Areolar Tissue: Located beneath the skin, between muscles, around blood vessels, nerves, and in bone marrow. Structure: Acts as a loose connective tissue matrix containing collagen and elastic fibres, with fibroblasts, macrophages, and mast cells. Function: Acts as a packing tissue between organs, helps repair damaged tissues, and fixes organs in place. 2. Adipose Tissue: Located beneath the skin, around internal organs like kidneys and heart. Structure: Composed of adipocytes (fat-storing cells) filled with large fat globules. Function: Acts as a fat reservoir, provides thermal insulation (prevents heat loss), and acts as a shock absorber to protect internal organs.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: In a microscopic observation of an onion root tip (meristematic tissue), a student counts a total of 250 cells in a field of view. Out of these, 35 cells are observed to be in various stages of mitosis. Calculate the mitotic index of this meristematic tissue sample as a percentage.
answer_key: Mitotic Index = (Number of dividing cells / Total number of cells) * 100 = (35 / 250) * 100 = 0.14 * 100 = 14%. Final Answer: 14%.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: A student examines the lower epidermis of a leaf under a microscope. The area of the microscopic field of view is calculated to be 0.25 mm^2. If 18 stomata are counted within this field of view, calculate the stomatal density per mm^2.
answer_key: Stomatal Density = Number of stomata / Area of field of view = 18 / 0.25 = 72 stomata/mm^2. Final Answer: 72 stomata per mm^2.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Under a compound microscope with a total magnification of 400x, the image of a parenchyma cell measures 24 mm in length on the micrometer scale. Calculate the actual length of the parenchyma cell in micrometres (um).
answer_key: Actual Size = Image Size / Magnification = 24 mm / 400 = 0.06 mm. Converting to micrometres (1 mm = 1000 um): 0.06 * 1000 = 60 um. Final Answer: 60 um.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: A transverse section of a dicot stem shows a xylem vessel with an outer circular diameter of 80 um and a wall thickness of 15 um. Calculate the inner lumen diameter of this xylem vessel in micrometres.
answer_key: Inner lumen diameter = Outer diameter - (2 * wall thickness) = 80 - (2 * 15) = 80 - 30 = 50 um. Final Answer: 50 um.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: In a cross-section of a herbaceous stem, the total area of the stem is 120 mm^2. If the pith occupies 36 mm^2, the vascular bundles occupy 48 mm^2, and the remaining area is cortex, calculate the percentage of the stem area occupied by the vascular bundles.
answer_key: Percentage = (Area of vascular bundles / Total stem area) * 100 = (48 / 120) * 100 = 0.4 * 100 = 40%. Final Answer: 40%.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: A multinucleated striated (skeletal) muscle fiber viewed under a high-power microscope has a total length of 1.2 mm. If nuclei are distributed at an average linear density of 25 nuclei per millimeter along the fiber, calculate the total number of nuclei present in this muscle fiber.
answer_key: Total nuclei = Fiber length * Nuclei density = 1.2 mm * 25 nuclei/mm = 30 nuclei. Final Answer: 30 nuclei.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: A standard hemocytometer count of human blood (fluid connective tissue) shows an average count of 50 red blood cells (RBCs) in a small grid volume of 0.0002 mm^3. Calculate the concentration of RBCs per mm^3 of blood.
answer_key: RBC concentration per mm^3 = Cell count / Grid volume = 50 / 0.0002 = 250,000 cells/mm^3. Final Answer: 250,000 cells/mm^3.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: A dry sample of compact bone tissue weighs 150 grams. Upon chemical analysis, it is found that organic components (such as ossein protein) make up 35% of the dry weight, while inorganic salts (calcium and phosphorus compounds) make up the rest. Calculate the weight of the inorganic mineral component in grams.
answer_key: Inorganic percentage = 100% - 35% = 65%. Weight of inorganic component = 65% of 150 g = (65 / 100) * 150 = 97.5 grams. Final Answer: 97.5 g.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: A histological cross-section of a grey matter region in the brain (nervous tissue) with an area of 0.5 mm^2 contains 120 neuron cell bodies. Calculate the numerical density of neurons per mm^2.
answer_key: Neuron density = Number of neurons / Area = 120 / 0.5 = 240 neurons/mm^2. Final Answer: 240 neurons/mm^2.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: An adipose tissue sample contains 8,000 adipocytes (fat cells). If each adipocyte stores an average of 0.000005 mg of fat lipid, calculate the total mass of stored fat in this tissue sample in milligrams (mg).
answer_key: Total fat mass = Number of adipocytes * Fat per cell = 8,000 * 0.000005 mg = 0.04 mg. Final Answer: 0.04 mg.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the following passage and answer the questions below:
A student is observing a longitudinal section of an onion root tip under a compound microscope. He notices a region near the apex where cells are densely packed, have prominent nuclei, abundant cytoplasm, and lack intercellular spaces. Further away from the apex, cells show elongation and vacuolation.
(a) Identify the specific plant tissue found at the apex of the root tip.
(b) State two structural features of these actively dividing cells that help them perform their function.
(c) Explain what happens to the cells as they move away from the apical region.
answer_key: (a) Apical meristematic tissue. (b) Features: Prominent nuclei and dense cytoplasm for high metabolic activity; absence of intercellular spaces and thin cellulosic cell walls. (c) As cells move away from the apical region, they undergo differentiation and maturation, developing large central vacuoles, thickened cell walls, and specific structural adaptations to form permanent tissues.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the following passage and answer the questions below:
While examining a transverse section of a sunflower stem in a biology laboratory, Rohini observes three distinct types of simple permanent tissues: one providing flexibility, one providing mechanical strength with dead cells, and one involved in food storage.
(a) Identify the tissue responsible for providing flexibility to bending plant parts like leaf stalks.
(b) Name the dead, lignified tissue that provides mechanical strength and rigidity to the plant stem.
(c) Differentiate between these two tissues based on cell viability and the nature of their cell wall thickening.
answer_key: (a) Collenchyma. (b) Sclerenchyma. (c) Collenchyma cells are living at maturity with uneven thickenings of cellulose and pectin at the corners. Sclerenchyma cells are dead at maturity with uniformly thickened, lignified secondary cell walls.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the following passage and answer the questions below:
Water and mineral absorption from roots must be transported to the farthest leaves of a tall eucalyptus tree, while synthesized food from leaves must reach the roots. This transport relies on complex permanent tissues.
(a) Name the complex permanent tissue responsible for upward conduction of water and minerals.
(b) Which element of this tissue is mainly responsible for the actual water conduction in angiosperms?
(c) Why are xylem and phloem referred to as 'complex tissues'?
answer_key: (a) Xylem. (b) Xylem vessels (or tracheids and vessels). (c) They are called complex tissues because they are made of more than one type of cell working together to perform a common specialized function.
rubric_keywords: more than one type of cell

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the following passage and answer the questions below:
The inner lining of the human intestine is specialized for absorption of digested food, featuring a single layer of tall, pillar-like cells with brush borders.
(a) Identify the specific epithelial tissue lining the intestine.
(b) State the primary function of this tissue in the intestine and name one other location where it is found.
(c) How does the presence of microvilli enhance the efficiency of this tissue?
answer_key: (a) Columnar epithelium. (b) Function: Absorption and secretion. Other location: Inner lining of the stomach or respiratory tract. (c) Microvilli drastically increase the surface area available for absorption of digested nutrients.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the following passage and answer the questions below:
A doctor examining an athlete who suffered a knee injury explains that the knee joint involves bones connected to each other, muscles attached to bones, and a cushion-like skeletal tissue providing smooth movement at the joint surfaces.
(a) Identify the connective tissue that connects two bones together at a joint.
(b) Name the smooth, elastic skeletal connective tissue found at the articulating ends of bones.
(c) Differentiate between tendons and ligaments based on their attachment roles.
answer_key: (a) Ligament. (b) Cartilage. (c) Ligaments connect bone to bone and are elastic/flexible, whereas tendons connect skeletal muscles to bones and are tough, inelastic fibrous tissues.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the following passage and answer the questions below:
Muscular tissue enables all kinds of body movements. While skeletal muscles help in walking and running, the heart beats continuously throughout life without getting fatigued, and the walls of the intestine regulate peristalsis involuntarily.
(a) Identify the type of muscular tissue found in the walls of the heart.
(b) Give two structural differences between skeletal muscle and smooth muscle.
(c) Why can cardiac muscle work continuously without fatigue?
answer_key: (a) Cardiac muscle tissue. (b) Skeletal muscles are striated, voluntary, and multinucleate with unbranched fibers; smooth muscles are unstriated, involuntary, spindle-shaped, and uninucleate. (c) Cardiac muscles have abundant mitochondria, a rich blood supply, and intercalated discs that allow rapid synchronous contractions without fatigue.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the following passage and answer the questions below:
When a person touches a hot object accidentally, sensory signals travel rapidly through specialized elongated cells to the spinal cord, triggering an immediate withdrawal reflex.
(a) Name the structural and functional unit of the nervous tissue involved in transmitting impulses.
(b) Identify the short, branched cytoplasmic extensions that receive impulses, and the long fiber that transmits impulses away from the cell body.
(c) What is the term given to the junction between two nerve cells where neurotransmitters relay the impulse?
answer_key: (a) Neuron (or nerve cell). (b) Dendrites (receive impulses) and Axon (transmits away). (c) Synapse.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the following passage and answer the questions below:
The epidermal layer of desert plants is often covered by a thick waxy coating, and the epidermis contains tiny pores regulated by specialized kidney-shaped cells.
(a) Name the waxy, water-resistant substance secreted by the epidermal cells in xerophytic plants.
(b) Identify the specialized epidermal cells that regulate the opening and closing of stomatal pores.
(c) State two primary functions of stomata in plants.
answer_key: (a) Cutin (forming the cuticle). (b) Guard cells. (c) Functions: gaseous exchange (oxygen and carbon dioxide) for respiration and photosynthesis, and transpiration (loss of water vapor for cooling and suction pull).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the following passage and answer the questions below:
Plant and animal tissues differ fundamentally in their organization and functional demands because plants are autotrophic and stationary, whereas animals are heterotrophic and mobile.
(a) Why do plants require more dead supportive tissues compared to animals?
(b) State one major difference in growth pattern between plant tissues and animal tissues.
(c) Name the fluid connective tissue in animals that transports respiratory gases, hormones, and nutrients.
answer_key: (a) Plants are stationary and need to bear upright structural loads against wind and gravity, requiring rigid dead mechanical tissues (like sclerenchyma). (b) Plant growth is restricted to specific regions (meristematic zones) and continues throughout life, whereas animal growth is uniform throughout the body and ceases after maturity. (c) Blood.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the following passage and answer the questions below:
Blood and bone are both vital connective tissues in vertebrates, yet their consistency and matrix properties are drastically different.
(a) What is the nature of the matrix found in bone tissue compared to blood tissue?
(b) Name the specialized bone-forming cells and the hard mineral salts that make the bone matrix rigid.
(c) How does the fluid matrix (plasma) of blood assist in its transport function?
answer_key: (a) Bone has a solid, rigid, calcified matrix, whereas blood has a liquid, non-rigid matrix called plasma. (b) Osteoblasts (or osteocytes); calcium and phosphorus salts (calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate). (c) Plasma is a watery fluid that dissolves and carries nutrients, hormones, wastes, and proteins throughout the circulatory system.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Which of the following is defined as a modified shoot wherein the shoot apex gets transformed into a floral meristem?
answer_key: A flower is defined as a modified shoot meant for sexual reproduction, where the internodes do not elongate and the floral leaves are arranged successively on the condensed axis (thalamus).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: The whorl of sepals in a flower is collectively known as:
answer_key: The calyx is the outermost non-essential whorl of a flower composed of individual units called sepals, which protect the flower in the bud stage.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Which part of the stamen produces pollen grains?
answer_key: The anther is the swollen, typically two-lobed terminal part of the stamen where pollen grains are produced inside pollen sacs.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: A flower that contains both male and female reproductive organs is termed as:
answer_key: A bisexual (or hermaphrodite) flower contains both androecium (male organs) and gynoecium (female organs) in the same flower.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant is called:
answer_key: Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or a genetically identical flower on the same plant.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: What is the term used for flowers that never open and strictly undergo self-pollination?
answer_key: Cleistogamous flowers remain permanently closed, ensuring guaranteed self-pollination without the need for external pollinating agents.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Which of the following parts of a carpel receives the pollen grains during pollination?
answer_key: The stigma is the sticky terminal receptive surface of the carpel/pistil designed to catch and hold pollen grains.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: In flowers pollinated by wind (anemophilous), the pollen grains are typically:
options: Light, dry, and produced in large quantities
answer_key: Wind-pollinated flowers produce light, dry, and non-sticky pollen grains in enormous quantities so they can be easily carried away by air currents.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Fusion of male gamete with the female egg cell inside the embryo sac is known as:
answer_key: Syngamy is the true fusion of the male gamete with the female egg cell to form a diploid zygote.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: After fertilization, what does the ovule develop into?
answer_key: After fertilization, the fertilized ovule develops into a seed, while the ovary matures into the fruit.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: The swollen tip of the pedicel upon which the four floral whorls are arranged is called the ___.
answer_key: Thalamus (or Receptacle). Explanation: The thalamus is the modified shoot apex that bears the floral leaves.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Flowers containing both male and female reproductive organs are known as bisexual or ___ flowers.
answer_key: Hermaphrodite. Explanation: A flower having both androecium and gynoecium is called bisexual or hermaphrodite.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: The non-essential accessory whorls of a flower that protect the inner reproductive organs in the bud condition are the calyx and the ___.
answer_key: Corolla. Explanation: Calyx (sepals) and corolla (petals) are non-essential/accessory whorls, whereas androecium and gynoecium are essential whorls.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: A condition where stamens are fused with each other by their filaments into a single bundle, as seen in China rose, is called ___.
answer_key: Monadelphous. Explanation: In monadelphous condition, all filaments are united into a single bundle or tube.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant is called ___.
answer_key: Self-pollination (or Autogamy / Geitonogamy). Explanation: Self-pollination involves transfer of pollen within the same plant or flower.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Insect-pollinated flowers are specifically referred to as ___ flowers.
answer_key: Entomophilous. Explanation: Flowers pollinated by insects are entomophilous and typically possess brightly colored petals, nectar, and scented flowers.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: In a flower where the ovary is situated below the attachment of calyx, corolla, and androecium, the ovary is described as ___.
answer_key: Inferior. Explanation: In an epigynous flower, the thalamus grows upward enclosing the ovary, making the ovary inferior.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: The fusion of a male gamete with the egg cell inside the embryo sac is known as ___.
answer_key: Syngamy (or Fertilization). Explanation: Syngamy is the true fertilization resulting in the formation of a diploid zygote.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: After fertilization, the integuments of the ovule develop into the protective seed ___.
answer_key: Coat (Testa and Tegmen). Explanation: The outer integument becomes the testa and the inner integument becomes the tegmen, collectively forming the seed coat.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Wind-pollinated flowers, such as maize and grasses, are known as ___ flowers.
answer_key: Anemophilous. Explanation: Anemophilous flowers are pollinated by wind and usually produce light, dry, and numerous pollen grains with feathery stigmas.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Define a flower. State its primary biological significance.
answer_key: A flower is defined as a modified shoot meant for sexual reproduction in angiosperms. Its primary biological significance is to produce haploid gametes (pollen grains and egg cells) and facilitate fertilization to form seeds and fruits, ensuring the continuity of the species.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Distinguish between a complete flower and an incomplete flower with an example of each.
answer_key: A complete flower possesses all four floral whorls (calyx, corolla, androecium, and gynoecium), e.g., China rose (Hibiscus). An incomplete flower lacks one or more of these four floral whorls, e.g., Cucumber or Maize flower.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: What is placentation? Name any two types of placentation found in flowering plants.
answer_key: Placentation is the manner in which ovules are arranged or attached inside the ovary. Two common types are marginal placentation (e.g., pea) and axile placentation (e.g., tomato or China rose).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Differentiate between self-pollination and cross-pollination. Give one advantage of cross-pollination.
answer_key: Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant. Cross-pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a flower on one plant to the stigma of a flower on another plant of the same species. Advantage: Cross-pollination introduces genetic variations, leading to healthier and more adaptable offspring.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: What are bracts? State their primary function in a plant.
answer_key: Bracts are specialized, modified leaf-like structures at the base of which a flower or an inflorescence arises. Their primary function is to protect the young flower bud during its early development.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Explain the term 'epicalyx'. In which plant family is it commonly observed?
answer_key: An epicalyx is an additional whorl of green, leaf-like bracteoles situated just outside the true calyx in certain flowers. It is commonly observed in the Malvaceae family (e.g., China rose).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Differentiate between unisexual and bisexual flowers, giving one example of each.
answer_key: A unisexual flower contains either only stamens (male) or only carpels (female), e.g., Papaya or Maize. A bisexual flower contains both stamens and carpels in the same flower, e.g., Mustard or China rose.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: What is the role of the calyx and corolla in a flower?
answer_key: The calyx (sepals) protects the inner floral whorls in the bud stage and performs photosynthesis when green. The corolla (petals) is brightly colored and scented to attract insects and other animal pollinators for pollination.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Define pollination. Name the two main abiotic agents of pollination.
answer_key: Pollination is defined as the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower. The two main abiotic agents of pollination are wind (anemophily) and water (hydrophily).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: What is meant by syngamy in angiosperms? Where does it take place?
answer_key: Syngamy is the fusion of the male gamete (nucleus) with the female gamete (egg cell/ovum) to form a diploid zygote. It takes place inside the embryo sac located within the ovule of the ovary.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Match the floral whorls in Column I with their respective basic units in Column II:
Column I:
1. Calyx
2. Corolla
3. Androecium
4. Gynoecium

Column II:
A. Petals
B. Carpels / Pistils
C. Sepals
D. Stamens
answer_key: 1-C, 2-A, 3-D, 4-B. Calyx consists of sepals; corolla consists of petals; androecium consists of stamens; gynoecium consists of carpels.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Match the types of pollination in Column I with their respective agents in Column II:
Column I:
1. Anemophily
2. Entomophily
3. Ornithophily
4. Hydrophily

Column II:
A. Pollination by insects
B. Pollination by wind
C. Pollination by water
D. Pollination by birds
answer_key: 1-B, 2-A, 3-D, 4-C. Anemophily is wind pollination, entomophily is insect pollination, ornithophily is bird pollination, and hydrophily is water pollination.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Match the types of placentation in Column I with their descriptions in Column II:
Column I:
1. Marginal placentation
2. Axile placentation
3. Parietal placentation
4. Free central placentation

Column II:
A. Ovules are borne on the central axis in a multilocular ovary
B. Ovules are borne on the inner wall of a unilocular ovary
C. Ovules are borne on the ventral suture of a unilocular ovary
D. Ovules are borne on a central axis without septa in a unilocular ovary
answer_key: 1-C, 2-A, 3-B, 4-D. Marginal placentation has ovules on the ventral suture; axile has ovules on central axis in multilocular ovary; parietal has ovules on inner wall; free central has ovules on central axis without septa.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Match the floral structures before fertilization in Column I with their post-fertilization derivatives in Column II:
Column I:
1. Ovary
2. Ovule
3. Outer integument
4. Inner integument

Column II:
A. Testa
B. Tegmen
C. Seed
D. Fruit
answer_key: 1-D, 2-C, 3-A, 4-B. Ovary develops into fruit; ovule develops into seed; outer integument forms testa; inner integument forms tegmen.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Match the flower types in Column I with their appropriate definitions in Column II:
Column I:
1. Bisexual flower
2. Unisexual flower
3. Complete flower
4. Neuter flower

Column II:
A. A flower lacking both androecium and gynoecium
B. A flower having both androecium and gynoecium
C. A flower having either androecium or gynoecium
D. A flower possessing all four floral whorls
answer_key: 1-B, 2-C, 3-D, 4-A. Bisexual flowers contain both stamens and carpels; unisexual contain either; complete flowers possess all four whorls; neuter flowers lack essential reproductive organs.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Match the adaptations of wind-pollinated flowers in Column I with their features in Column II:
Column I:
1. Stigma
2. Pollen grains
3. Stamens
4. Petals

Column II:
A. Long, protruding, and feathery to catch pollen
B. Small, inconspicuous, often dull-colored or greenish
C. Light, dry, and produced in large numbers
D. Long and dangling to release pollen in the wind
answer_key: 1-A, 2-C, 3-D, 4-B. Stigma is feathery and protruding; pollen grains are light and dry; stamens are long and dangling; petals are small and inconspicuous.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Match the parts of a typical pistil in Column I with their descriptions in Column II:
Column I:
1. Stigma
2. Style
3. Ovary
4. Ovule

Column II:
A. The swollen basal part containing ovules
B. The terminal sticky surface for receiving pollen grains
C. The structure enclosing the embryo sac
D. The elongated tubular stalk connecting stigma and ovary
answer_key: 1-B, 2-D, 3-A, 4-C. Stigma receives pollen; style connects stigma to ovary; ovary is the basal swollen part; ovule contains the embryo sac.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Match the insect-pollinated flower features in Column I with their functions in Column II:
Column I:
1. Petals
2. Nectaries
3. Pollen grains
4. Stigma

Column II:
A. Sticky or spiny to easily adhere to insect bodies
B. Brightly colored, large, and scented to attract insects
C. Sticky or rough so pollen sticks upon contact
D. Secrete sweet nectar as a reward for pollinators
answer_key: 1-B, 2-D, 3-A, 4-C. Entomophilous flowers have brightly colored scented petals, nectaries for nectar, sticky/spiny pollen grains, and sticky/rough stigmas.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Match the floral symmetry types in Column I with their definitions in Column II:
Column I:
1. Actinomorphic
2. Zygomorphic
3. Asymmetric

Column II:
A. Bilaterally symmetrical, divisible into two equal halves in only one plane
B. Radially symmetrical, divisible into two equal halves in any radial plane
C. Irregular, cannot be divided into two equal halves in any plane
answer_key: 1-B, 2-A, 3-C. Actinomorphic flowers are radially symmetrical; zygomorphic are bilaterally symmetrical; asymmetric flowers cannot be divided symmetrically in any plane.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Match the fertilization terms in Column I with their descriptions in Column II:
Column I:
1. Syngamy
2. Triple fusion
3. Primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)
4. Zygote

Column II:
A. Formed by fusion of male gamete and secondary nucleus (3n)
B. Develops into the embryo (2n)
C. Fusion of male gamete with the egg cell
D. Triploid nucleus that divides to form nutritive endosperm tissue
answer_key: 1-C, 2-A, 3-D, 4-B. Syngamy is fusion with egg cell; triple fusion is fusion with secondary nucleus; PEN is triploid nucleus forming endosperm; zygote develops into embryo.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Assertion (A): A typical flower has four whorls arranged on the swollen end of the pedicel called the thalamus.
Reason (R): The calyx and corolla are essential whorls directly involved in sexual reproduction.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
answer_key:
Answer: A is true, but R is false.
Explanation: A typical flower possesses four whorls (calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium) inserted on the thalamus. Calyx and corolla are accessory (non-essential) whorls for protection and attraction, whereas androecium and gynoecium are essential whorls directly involved in reproduction.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Assertion (A): Wind-pollinated flowers typically produce a very large quantity of light, smooth, and dry pollen grains.
Reason (R): Wind pollination is a haphazard process, and heavy pollen grains would fail to be transported efficiently over long distances by air currents.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
answer_key:
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Explanation: Anemophilous (wind-pollinated) flowers produce lightweight, dry, and abundant pollen grains because wind pollination is a random process with high wastage, requiring massive output and easy airborne transport.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Assertion (A): The calyx provides protection to the inner delicate floral whorls during the bud stage.
Reason (R): Sepals are typically green, leaf-like structures that enclose the flower bud before it opens.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
answer_key:
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Explanation: The calyx consists of individual units called sepals, which are generally green and leaf-like. Their primary function is to protect the inner petals, stamens, and carpels when the flower is in its developmental bud stage.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Assertion (A): Unisexual flowers are incapable of ever undergoing self-pollination.
Reason (R): Unisexual flowers contain either only stamens or only pistils, making pollen transfer from the anther to the stigma of the same flower structurally impossible.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
answer_key:
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Explanation: A unisexual flower lacks either male or female organs. Thus, self-pollination within the same flower cannot occur, although self-pollination can still occur between different flowers on the same plant (geitonogamy) if it is monoecious.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Assertion (A): After successful fertilization, the ovary of the flower develops into a fruit and the ovules develop into seeds.
Reason (R): The ovary wall transforms into the pericarp, which serves to protect the developing seeds.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
answer_key:
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Explanation: Post-fertilization changes in a flower include the transformation of the ovary into the fruit, ovules into seeds, and the ovary wall into the pericarp (fruit wall) which protects the seeds.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Assertion (A): Stamens constitute the female reproductive whorl of a flowering plant.
Reason (R): Each stamen is composed of a filament and an anther that houses pollen grains.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
answer_key:
Answer: A is false, but R is true.
Explanation: The stamen is the male reproductive whorl (androecium), not the female reproductive whorl. The reason correctly describes the parts and function of a stamen (filament and anther producing pollen grains).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Assertion (A): Insect-pollinated (entomophilous) flowers often possess brightly colored petals, pleasant fragrances, and nectar.
Reason (R): These characteristics act as visual and chemical attractants to guide pollinators like insects to the flower.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
answer_key:
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Explanation: Entomophilous flowers rely on biotic agents. Bright corollas, scent, and nectar reward insects, ensuring effective visits and subsequent transfer of pollen grains.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Assertion (A): Cross-pollination is genetically superior to self-pollination because it introduces variations in offspring.
Reason (R): Cross-pollination involves the fusion of male and female gametes derived from flowers on two entirely different plants of the same species.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
answer_key:
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Explanation: Cross-pollination (xenogamy) brings together genetic material from two different parent plants, promoting genetic recombination, adaptability, and healthier offspring compared to continuous self-pollination.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Assertion (A): The stigma is the swollen basal part of the carpel that receives pollen grains during pollination.
Reason (R): The style connects the stigma to the ovary.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
answer_key:
Answer: A is false, but R is true.
Explanation: The stigma is the terminal, sticky upper part of the carpel that receives pollen, not the basal part. The ovary is the swollen basal part containing ovules. The reason correctly describes the role of the style.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Assertion (A): Placentation refers to the manner in which ovules are arranged inside the ovary of a flower.
Reason (R): Different types of placentation, such as marginal, axile, and parietal, help in classifying floral structures and aid in seed distribution.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
answer_key:
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Explanation: Placentation is precisely the arrangement of ovules within the ovary. The various types (marginal, axile, parietal, free-central, basal) are significant taxonomic features and affect how seeds are housed and released.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Describe the structure of a typical bisexual flower, detailing its four distinct floral whorls and their arrangement on the thalamus.
answer_key: A typical bisexual flower consists of four main floral whorls arranged successively on a swollen end of the pedicel called the thalamus or receptacle. 1. Calyx (Outermost whorl): Composed of green leaf-like structures called sepals. It protects the flower in the bud stage and performs photosynthesis if green. 2. Corolla (Second whorl): Composed of brightly colored or scented petals. Its primary function is to attract insects for pollination and protect the inner reproductive organs. 3. Androecium (Third whorl): The male reproductive whorl consisting of stamens. Each stamen has a slender stalk called a filament and an anther that produces pollen grains. 4. Gynoecium or Pistil (Innermost whorl): The female reproductive whorl consisting of one or more carpels. Each carpel is divided into three parts: ovary (contains ovules), style (slender tube), and stigma (receptive surface for pollen).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Differentiate between essential and non-essential floral whorls. Explain the specific reproductive roles played by stamens and carpels.
answer_key: Non-essential (accessory) whorls include the calyx and corolla, which do not directly take part in sexual reproduction but protect the inner floral parts and attract pollinators. Essential whorls include the androecium and gynoecium, which take direct part in reproduction. Roles: Stamens (Androecium) produce microspores or pollen grains containing the male gametes necessary for fertilization. Carpels (Gynoecium) produce female gametes (egg cells/ova) within the ovules inside the ovary, provide a surface for pollen germination, and later develop into fruit and seeds after fertilization.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Define pollination. Distinguish between self-pollination and cross-pollination, and state any four major advantages of cross-pollination over self-pollination.
answer_key: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a flower to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same species. Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant. Cross-pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther of a flower on one plant to the stigma of a flower on another plant of the same species. Four advantages of cross-pollination: 1. Produces healthier and more vigorous offspring due to genetic recombination. 2. Seeds produced are usually larger and viable. 3. New varieties and desirable traits can be introduced. 4. Offspring show better adaptability and resistance to diseases and environmental changes.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Compare the structural adaptations of insect-pollinated (entomophilous) flowers with wind-pollinated (anemophilous) flowers, giving five distinct differences.
answer_key: Five structural differences: 1. Petals: Insect-pollinated flowers have large, brightly colored, and conspicuous petals; wind-pollinated flowers have small, dull, or inconspicuous petals (often lacking color/nectar). 2. Nectar and Odor: Insect-pollinated flowers produce nectar and sweet fragrance to attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers do not produce nectar or scent. 3. Pollen grains: Insect-pollinated flowers produce sticky, spiny, or rough pollen grains that adhere to insect bodies; wind-pollinated flowers produce light, dry, smooth, and abundant pollen grains easily carried by wind. 4. Stamens: Insect-pollinated flowers have stamens enclosed within the flower; wind-pollinated flowers have long, dangling stamens with versatile anthers exposed to air currents. 5. Stigma: Insect-pollinated flowers have sticky, compact stigmas inside the flower; wind-pollinated flowers have large, feathery, or sticky protruding stigmas to trap airborne pollen effectively.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Describe the complete process of fertilization in flowering plants starting from the arrival of pollen on the stigma until the fusion of gametes.
answer_key: 1. Pollen deposition: Pollen grains land on the sticky surface of a compatible stigma. 2. Germination: The pollen grain absorbs moisture and sugar from the stigma and germinates to form a pollen tube. 3. Pollen tube growth: The pollen tube grows down through the style carrying two male gametes (or a generative nucleus dividing into two male gametes and a tube nucleus). 4. Entry into ovule: The pollen tube enters the ovary and reaches the ovule through a tiny pore called the micropyle. 5. Fusion of gametes (Syngamy): The tip of the pollen tube bursts, releasing the male gametes into the embryo sac. One male gamete fuses with the egg cell (female gamete) to form a diploid zygote, which subsequently develops into an embryo.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Explain the terms: (a) Complete flower, (b) Incomplete flower, (c) Bisexual flower, (d) Unisexual flower, (e) Neuter flower, with suitable examples for each.
answer_key: (a) Complete flower: A flower that possesses all four floral whorls (calyx, corolla, androecium, and gynoecium). Example: Hibiscus, Mustard. (b) Incomplete flower: A flower in which one or more of the four floral whorls are missing. Example: Cucumber, Maize. (c) Bisexual (hermaphrodite) flower: A flower containing both male (androecium) and female (gynoecium) reproductive organs. Example: Pea, Mustard, Hibiscus. (d) Unisexual flower: A flower containing either only male organs (staminate) or only female organs (pistillate). Example: Papaya, Cucumber, Date palm. (e) Neuter flower: A sterile flower in which both androecium and gynoecium are absent or non-functional. Example: Ray florets of sunflower.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: What mechanisms or floral adaptations do plants possess to ensure cross-pollination and prevent self-pollination? Explain any four.
answer_key: Plants employ several mechanisms to discourage self-pollination and promote cross-pollination: 1. Dicliny (Unisexuality): Flowers are either male or female on the same plant (monoecious) or different plants (dioecious), making self-pollination impossible. Example: Papaya, Mulberry. 2. Dichogamy: The male and female reproductive organs mature at different times. If anthers mature earlier, it is protandry (e.g., Sunflower); if stigmas mature earlier, it is protogyny (e.g., Gloriosa). 3. Self-sterility (Self-incompatibility): Pollen from a flower is genetically unable to germinate or grow on the stigma of the same flower or plant. Example: Apple, Potato. 4. Herkogamy: A structural barrier exists between the anther and stigma in a bisexual flower, preventing self-transfer of pollen. Example: Gloriosa.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Trace the post-fertilization changes that occur in a flower, explaining how various parts of the flower transform into fruit and seed structures.
answer_key: Following fertilization, several profound structural and chemical changes occur in the flower: 1. Ovary: Grows rapidly, accumulates nutrients, and develops into the fruit. The ovary wall becomes the fruit wall (pericarp). 2. Ovules: Each fertilized ovule develops into a seed. 3. Zygote: Divides repeatedly by mitosis to form the embryo (future plant). 4. Integuments of the ovule: The outer and inner integuments harden and thicken to form the seed coat (testa and tegmen). 5. Other floral parts: Sepals, petals, stamens, style, and stigma usually wither, dry up, and fall off (though in some cases like brinjal or tomato, sepals persist).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Explain the significance of artificial pollination. Describe the steps involved in artificial hybridization in crop plants.
answer_key: Artificial pollination involves the manual transfer of pollen from the anthers of a desired male parent plant to the stigma of a selected female parent plant. Significance: It is widely used by plant breeders to combine desirable traits (such as high yield, disease resistance, and climate resilience) from two different varieties to produce superior hybrid varieties. Steps in artificial hybridization: 1. Emasculation: Removal of stamens (anthers) from an unopened bisexual flower bud of the female parent to prevent self-pollination. 2. Bagging: The emasculated flower is covered with a butter-paper or polythene bag to prevent contamination by unwanted foreign pollen. 3. Dusting: When the stigma matures, mature pollen from the selected male parent is dusted onto the stigma manually using a brush. 4. Re-bagging: The flower is bagged again until seeds develop so that true hybrid seeds can be harvested.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Describe the structure of a mature seed with reference to a bean seed (dicot seed) and a maize grain (monocot grain), highlighting key differences.
answer_key: A mature seed is a fertilized, ripened ovule containing an embryo and stored food. 1. Dicot seed (e.g., Bean seed): Covered by a protective seed coat with a scar called the hilum and a micropyle. It contains an embryo consisting of two fleshy cotyledons (store food), an embryonic axis with a radicle (future root), and a plumule (future shoot). It lacks endosperm at maturity (non-endospermic). 2. Monocot grain (e.g., Maize grain): Technically a fruit (caryopsis) where the seed coat is fused with the fruit wall. It contains a single cotyledon called scutellum. Food is stored in a separate bulky endosperm tissue. The embryo has a radicle protected by a sheath (coleorhiza) and a plumule protected by a sheath (coleoptile).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: A typical pentamerous flower has 5 sepals, 5 petals, 10 stamens, and 5 carpels. If a branch bears 12 such flowers, calculate the total number of stamens present on the branch.
answer_key: Total number of stamens = Number of flowers × Stamens per flower = 12 × 10 = 120 stamens.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: An anther lobe contains 25 microspore mother cells (pollen mother cells). Assuming each pollen mother cell undergoes meiosis to form 4 pollen grains and each pollen grain produces 2 male gametes, calculate the total number of male gametes produced.
answer_key: 1 PMC undergoes meiosis to form 4 pollen grains. Total pollen grains = 25 × 4 = 100. Each pollen grain produces 2 male gametes. Total male gametes = 100 × 2 = 200.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: An ovary of a flower contains 15 carpels, with each carpel having 4 ovules. After successful fertilization, if 80% of the ovules develop into seeds, calculate the total number of seeds formed in that ovary.
answer_key: Total ovules = 15 × 4 = 60. Seeds formed = 60 × 0.80 = 48 seeds.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: In a hypogynous flower, the ratio of sepals to petals to stamens is 1:1:3. If the total number of floral leaves in the calyx, corolla, and androecium combined is 25, find the number of stamens.
answer_key: Let parts be x, x, and 3x. Sum = x + x + 3x = 5x = 25, so x = 5. Number of stamens = 3x = 3 × 5 = 15.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: In a laboratory experiment on pollen germination, 250 pollen grains were dusted on a nutrient medium. Out of these, 175 pollen grains successfully germinated to produce pollen tubes. Calculate the percentage germination of pollen grains.
answer_key: Percentage germination = (Germinated pollen / Total pollen) × 100 = (175 / 250) × 100 = 70%.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: A researcher examines 8 complete flowers of a plant species. Each flower possesses 4 sepals and 4 petals in its non-reproductive whorls. What is the total number of non-reproductive floral leaves (sepals and petals combined) across all 8 flowers?
answer_key: Non-reproductive floral leaves per flower = Sepals + Petals = 4 + 4 = 8. Total for 8 flowers = 8 × 8 = 64.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Each of the 4 pollen sacs in an anther contains 120 microspore mother cells. If a flower has 6 stamens (each containing a dithecous anther with 4 pollen sacs), calculate the total number of microspore mother cells in the entire flower.
answer_key: Total PMC per flower = Stamens × Sacs per stamen × PMC per sac = 6 × 4 × 120 = 2,880.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: An inflorescence contains 45 flowers. If each flower has an ovary containing 6 ovules, and 50% of the total ovules fail to fertilize, calculate the total number of unfertilized ovules in the entire inflorescence.
answer_key: Total ovules = 45 × 6 = 270. Unfertilized ovules = 270 × 0.50 = 135.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: An actinomorphic flower has 5 petals. If you have a bouquet of 14 such flowers, calculate the total number of individual petals present in the bouquet.
answer_key: Total petals = 14 × 5 = 70 petals.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: In a hypogynous flower, the number of carpels is equal to one-third the number of stamens. If the flower has 15 stamens and the number of sepals and petals each equal the number of stamens, calculate the total sum of sepals, petals, stamens, and carpels.
answer_key: Stamens = 15. Carpels = 15 / 3 = 5. Sepals = 15, Petals = 15. Total sum = 15 + 15 + 15 + 5 = 50.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the given passage about a hibiscus flower observed by students in a biology laboratory and answer the questions that follow:
Students dissected a fresh Hibiscus rosa-sinensis flower and identified four distinct whorls arranged on the thalamus. The outermost green leaf-like structures protected the flower in the bud stage, followed by bright red petals that attracted pollinators. Inside the petals, numerous stamens fused into a staminal tube were observed, surrounding a central pistil with a five-lobed stigma.
(a) Name the outermost whorl and state its primary function.
(b) Differentiate between essential and non-essential floral whorls with reference to this flower.
answer_key:
(a) The outermost whorl is the calyx (composed of sepals). Its primary function is to protect the floral bud from mechanical injury and desiccation.
(b) Non-essential (accessory) whorls include the calyx and corolla, which only help in protection and attraction. Essential whorls include the androecium (stamens) and gynoecium (pistil), which take direct part in reproduction.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the case study on floral types and answer the questions:
During a botanical field trip, students encountered two types of plants: Plant A bearing flowers with both stamens and pistils, and Plant B bearing separate male flowers (staminate) and female flowers (pistillate) on the same plant body.
(a) Define Plant A type of flower and give one example.
(b) What term is used to describe Plant B condition where unisexual male and female flowers are borne on the same plant?
answer_key:
(a) Plant A bears a bisexual (hermaphrodite) flower because it contains both male (androecium) and female (gynoecium) reproductive organs. Example: Hibiscus, Pea, or Mustard.
(b) The condition where both male and female unisexual flowers are borne on the same plant is called monoecious (e.g., Maize, Cucumber).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the case study on floral symmetry and completeness:
In a study of angiosperm diversity, researchers examined a flower that lacked petals and sepals, possessing only reproductive organs protected by bracts, and exhibiting radial symmetry.
(a) What term is used to describe a flower that lacks one or more of the four floral whorls?
(b) Explain the significance of bracts in such flowers.
answer_key:
(a) An incomplete flower is one that lacks one or more of the four basic floral whorls (calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium).
(b) Bracts are modified leaves located at the base of the flower or flower stalk. In flowers lacking petals (apetalous flowers), bracts are often brightly colored or enlarged to perform the function of attracting pollinators.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the passage on androecium structure and answer the questions:
An observer studying the stamen under a microscope notes that each stamen consists of a slender filament and a bilobed anther containing powdery yellow grains.
(a) Name the powdery yellow grains produced inside the anther and state their role.
(b) What is the connective tissue in a stamen?
answer_key:
(a) The powdery yellow grains are pollen grains (microspores). They contain the male gametes responsible for sexual reproduction in flowering plants.
(b) The connective is a sterile strip of tissue that connects the two lobes of an anther together.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the case study on gynoecium and pistil structure:
The innermost whorl of a flower is the gynoecium, consisting of one or more carpels. A student dissected the ovary of a flower and observed tiny ovules attached to a cushion-like tissue inside.
(a) Name the cushion-like tissue inside the ovary where ovules are attached.
(b) List the three main parts of a typical carpel/pistil.
answer_key:
(a) The cushion-like tissue inside the ovary where ovules are attached is called the placenta, and the arrangement is termed placentation.
(b) The three main parts of a typical carpel (pistil) are the ovary (basal swollen part), style (elongated tube), and stigma (terminal sticky surface for receiving pollen).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the passage regarding pollination mechanisms in maize and rose:
Maize plants have lightweight, dry pollen grains and feathery exposed stigmas, whereas rose flowers are brightly colored, fragrant, and produce nectar.
(a) Identify the primary agent of pollination in maize and give its technical term.
(b) What type of pollination is facilitated by the floral adaptations seen in the rose flower?
answer_key:
(a) The primary agent of pollination in maize is wind, and flowers pollinated by wind are called anemophilous.
(b) The adaptations in rose (bright color, fragrance, nectar) facilitate entomophily (insect pollination).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the case study on fertilisation in flowering plants:
After pollen lands on a compatible stigma, it germinates to form a long tube that travels down the style towards the ovary containing ovules.
(a) What name is given to the tube formed by the germinating pollen grain?
(b) Describe what happens after the pollen tube enters the ovule (embryo sac).
answer_key:
(a) The tube formed by the germinating pollen grain is called the pollen tube.
(b) Upon entering the embryo sac, the pollen tube releases two male gametes. One male gamete fuses with the egg cell (syngamy) to form a zygote, and the other fuses with the secondary nucleus (triple fusion) to form the endosperm.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the passage on post-fertilisation changes in flowers:
Following successful fertilisation, significant structural transformations take place across the floral parts. The petals and stamens wither and fall off, while the ovary undergoes a remarkable transformation.
(a) What do the ovary and ovule transform into after fertilisation?
(b) What happens to the integuments of the ovule after fertilisation?
answer_key:
(a) After fertilisation, the ovary develops into the fruit, and the ovules develop into seeds.
(b) The integuments of the ovule harden and transform into the seed coats (testa and tegmen).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the case study on floral sexuality terms:
In a botanical survey of a garden, scientists cataloged different plant species based on whether their flowers contained male organs, female organs, or both.
(a) Distinguish between staminate and pistillate flowers.
(b) Give an example of a plant species that bears bisexual flowers.
answer_key:
(a) Staminate flowers are unisexual flowers that possess only stamens (male organs) and lack a functional pistil. Pistillate flowers are unisexual flowers that possess only a pistil (female organ) and lack functional stamens.
(b) Hibiscus, pea, mustard, or tomato are examples of plants bearing bisexual flowers.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question:
Read the passage on the significance of flowers:
Flowers are not only aesthetically pleasing and economically important in floriculture, but they are also crucial biological structures for plant propagation and genetic diversity.
(a) State two biological significances of flowers in plants.
(b) Name the branch of horticulture dealing with the cultivation of flowering plants.
answer_key:
(a) Two biological significances of flowers are: 1. They bear the reproductive organs necessary for sexual reproduction and seed formation. 2. They ensure genetic recombination and diversity through pollination.
(b) The branch of horticulture dealing with the cultivation of flowering plants is called floriculture.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant is known as:
answer_key: Self-pollination involves the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant. Therefore, option B is correct.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Which of the following characteristics is typically observed in wind-pollinated (anemophilous) flowers?
options: Brightly colored petals and strong fragrance
Light, dry, and non-sticky pollen grains
answer_key: Wind-pollinated flowers produce light, dry, and non-sticky pollen grains so they can be easily carried away by the wind. They usually lack bright petals, fragrance, and nectar.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: The fusion of a male gamete with the egg cell inside the embryo sac is called:
answer_key: Syngamy is the true fertilization process where a male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote. Triple fusion involves the second male gamete fusing with the polar nuclei.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: In flowering plants, double fertilization results in the formation of a zygote and:
answer_key: Double fertilization is unique to angiosperms. One male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form a zygote, and the second male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm, which nourishes the developing embryo.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Which part of the flower develops into the seed coat after fertilization?
answer_key: After fertilization, the integuments of the ovule develop into the tough protective seed coat (testa and tegmen). The ovary wall develops into the pericarp of the fruit.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Insect-pollinated flowers are generally characterized by:
options: Small, inconspicuous flowers with abundant dry pollen
Large, brightly colored petals, nectar, and sweet scent
Long dangling stamens and feathery stigmas
answer_key: Insect-pollinated (entomophilous) flowers possess adaptations such as brightly colored petals, pleasant scent, and nectar to attract insects, along with sticky or spiny pollen grains that adhere to the insect's body.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: What happens to the sepals, petals, and stamens in most flowers after fertilization takes place?
options: They grow larger and become part of the fruit
They remain permanently green and photosynthetic
answer_key: After fertilization, parts like sepals, petals, and stamens usually wither and fall off as their role in pollination is complete, while the ovary grows into the fruit.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: The pollen tube enters the ovule typically through a small opening known as the:
answer_key: The pollen tube enters the ovule through a tiny pore called the micropyle, which is located at the opposite end of the chalaza.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Cross-pollination between flowers of different plants of the same species is specifically referred to as:
answer_key: Xenogamy is true cross-pollination between flowers of different plants of the same species. Geitonogamy is pollination between different flowers of the same plant.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Which of the following is an example of a plant exhibiting artificial pollination?
options: Hand pollination in date palms or vanilla orchids by humans
answer_key: Artificial pollination involves human intervention where pollen is manually transferred from the anther to the stigma, commonly practiced in crops like date palms and vanilla orchids to ensure high yield.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower on the same plant is known as ___.
answer_key: Self-pollination. Rationale: Self-pollination involves pollen transfer within the same plant or flower without requiring external agents from other plants.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Insect-pollinated flowers typically possess brightly colored petals, a sweet scent, and ___ pollen grains to facilitate attachment to the insect's body.
answer_key: Sticky (or spiny). Rationale: Entomophilous flowers have sticky or rough pollen grains so they cling easily to visiting insects.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: The fusion of a male gamete with the female egg cell inside the embryo sac is called ___.
answer_key: Syngamy (or fertilization). Rationale: Syngamy is the true fertilization process resulting in the formation of a diploid zygote.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Following fertilization, the fertilized ovule transforms into a ___ and the mature ovary develops into a ___.
answer_key: Seed, fruit. Rationale: In angiosperms, the fertilized ovule becomes the seed and the ovary wall develops into the pericarp of the fruit.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Wind-pollinated flowers are characterized by lightweight, non-sticky pollen and large, feathery ___ designed to catch airborne pollen grains.
answer_key: Stigmas. Rationale: Anemophilous plants have exposed, feathery stigmas to maximize the surface area for trapping wind-carried pollen.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: The pollen tube usually enters the ovule through a tiny opening at the apex of the integuments known as the ___.
answer_key: Micropyle. Rationale: The micropyle is the small pore through which the pollen tube enters the embryo sac.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: The mode of cross-pollination effected by birds, typically seen in plants with tubular, brightly colored flowers, is called ___.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Define pollination. Name its two main types.
answer_key: Pollination is defined as the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same species. Its two main types are self-pollination and cross-pollination.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Differentiate between self-pollination and cross-pollination based on the genetic variation in offspring.
answer_key: In self-pollination, the offspring are genetically identical to the parent plant as there is no fusion of gametes from different genetic sources. In cross-pollination, the offspring show genetic variations because they receive genetic material from two different parent plants.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Mention two structural adaptations found in wind-pollinated (anemophilous) flowers.
answer_key: Two adaptations found in wind-pollinated flowers are: 1. They produce light, dry, and non-sticky pollen grains that can be easily carried by the wind. 2. They possess large, feathery, or sticky stigmas to easily trap pollen grains floating in the air.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: What is double fertilization? Name the two types of fusion events involved in it.
answer_key: Double fertilization is a unique process in flowering plants where two male gametes participate in fertilization inside the embryo sac. The two fusion events are: 1. Syneamy (fusion of one male gamete with the egg cell to form a zygote). 2. Triple fusion (fusion of the second male gamete with the secondary nucleus/polar nuclei to form the endosperm nucleus).

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: State any two advantages of cross-pollination over self-pollination.
answer_key: Two advantages of cross-pollination are: 1. The resulting seeds are more viable and produce healthier, more vigorous offspring. 2. It introduces genetic variations that help plants adapt better to changing environmental conditions and disease resistance.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Explain the role of the pollen tube in fertilization after pollination occurs.
answer_key: After a pollen grain lands on a compatible stigma, it germinates to form a pollen tube. The pollen tube grows down through the style, carrying the male gametes inside it, and enters the ovule through the micropyle to deliver the male gametes directly to the embryo sac for fertilization.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Give reasons why insect-pollinated flowers are brightly coloured and scented.
answer_key: Insect-pollinated flowers are brightly coloured and produce sweet scent or nectar to attract insects (like bees, butterflies) which act as agents of pollination, helping transfer pollen grains from one flower to another.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: What happens to the ovule and the ovary after fertilization takes place in a flowering plant?
answer_key: After fertilization, the ovule develops and transforms into a seed, while the ovary matures and enlarges to form the fruit of the plant.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Differentiate between entomophilous and ornithophilous flowers with one example for each.
answer_key: Entomophilous flowers are pollinated by insects (e.g., Rose, Jasmine) and are typically brightly colored with nectar and scent. Ornithophilous flowers are pollinated by birds (e.g., Butea, Bombax) and are usually tubular, brightly colored with large quantities of watery nectar but lack a prominent scent.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Define artificial pollination. State its significance in agriculture and horticulture.
answer_key: Artificial pollination is the man-made process of transferring pollen grains from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another desired flower. Its significance includes producing superior quality hybrid crops, improving crop yield, and developing disease-resistant plant varieties.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Differentiate between self-pollination and cross-pollination. State any four advantages and two disadvantages of cross-pollination.
answer_key: Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant. Cross-pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a flower on one plant to the stigma of a flower on another plant of the same species. Advantages of cross-pollination: (1) Produces healthier, more vigorous offspring due to genetic recombination, (2) Seeds produced are larger and more viable, (3) New varieties with desirable traits can be created, (4) Resistance to diseases and adverse environmental conditions increases. Disadvantages: (1) Highly wasteful as large quantities of pollen grains are required, (2) Completely dependent on external agents like wind, insects, or water.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Describe the four floral whorls of a typical bisexual flower, categorizing them into essential and non-essential whorls with their respective functions.
answer_key: A typical bisexual flower consists of four concentric whorls arranged on the thalamus: 1. Calyx (outermost whorl): Composed of sepals, usually green, protects the flower in the bud stage. 2. Corolla: Composed of petals, often brightly colored and scented to attract insects for pollination. Together, calyx and corolla form the non-essential or accessory whorls as they do not directly take part in reproduction. 3. Androecium: The male reproductive whorl composed of stamens, each having an anther and filament. It produces pollen grains containing male gametes. 4. Gynoecium (or Pistil): The female reproductive whorl composed of carpels (stigma, style, ovary). It produces female gametes (ovules). Androecium and gynoecium form the essential whorls as they are directly involved in sexual reproduction.

subject: Biology (Science Paper 3)
seed_question: Differentiate clearly between wind-pollinated (anemophilous) and insect-pollinated (entomophilous) flowers by giving five distinct structural differences.
answer_key: Differences between wind-pollinated and insect-pollinated flowers: 1. Petals: Insect-pollinated have large, brightly colored petals to attract insects; wind-pollinated have small, dull, inconspicuous petals or lack them entirely. 2. Nectar and Odor: Insect-pollinated produce nectar and pleasant scent; wind-pollinated do not produce nectar or scent. 3.
